meta.title: Ceres Power — Phil Caldwell's solid oxide fuel cell licensing model from Horsham through Bosch, Doosan, Weichai, Shell partnerships
meta.abstract: Ceres Power Holdings plc is a UK clean-energy technology company listed on the London Stock Exchange AIM (CWR.L) developing solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) and solid oxide electrolyser cell (SOEC) technology — its principal commercial model is licensing the SteelCell platform to global manufacturing partners including Bosch (Germany), Doosan (Korea), Weichai Power (China), and partnership with Shell on green hydrogen electrolysis. Headquartered in Horsham UK with the principal engineering site in Redhill UK. CEO Phil Caldwell has led the company through the licensing-model strategic pivot.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## Capital-Light on AIM

Ceres Power Holdings plc occupies a defined and narrow position in the energy transition: it owns the intellectual property for a metal-supported solid oxide fuel cell and electrolyser platform, licenses that technology to industrial partners, and does not itself build the gigafactories. Traded on London's AIM market under the ticker **CWR.L**, the company is headquartered in Horsham, West Sussex, with its engineering function in Redhill, Surrey. Phil Caldwell, chief executive since 2013, has managed the company through the full arc of what he calls the transition from upfront licence fees to recurring royalty revenue — the moment when a licensee's manufacturing volumes become large enough to generate a stream of per-unit payments that compounds without further capital from Ceres.

The company traces to a 2001 spin-out from Imperial College London, where the metal-supported cell design — operating at lower temperatures than the brittle ceramics used by earlier-generation solid oxide systems — was developed as a route to lower manufacturing cost and greater operational robustness.

## Four Partners, One Defection

For most of its commercial life, Ceres organised its licensing architecture around four relationships: **Bosch** (Germany, stationary SOFC), **Doosan** (South Korea, stationary power), **Weichai Power** (China, distributed power), and **Shell** (solid oxide electrolyser, green hydrogen). By the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, the structure had been partially remade.

In February 2025, Robert Bosch GmbH disclosed it would cease development of SOFC cells and stacks for manufacture, citing a broader strategic reorientation. Bosch held a 17.44% equity stake in Ceres acquired through the partnership and indicated it was considering a disposal. Caldwell's public statement acknowledged the loss without disputing Bosch's rationale:

> "Whilst Ceres is disappointed that Bosch will discontinue its operations relating to the industrialisation and preparation for production of decentralised power-supply systems using Ceres' solid oxide technology, we recognise that this decision is part of a broader revised strategic direction from Bosch and does not reflect its confidence around Ceres or our technology."

The direct revenue impact was confined to low single-digit millions of euros for 2025. The strategic impact was sharper: Bosch had been the company's most visible European industrial anchor, and the announcement triggered an immediate share-price decline. Ceres moved to fill the vacancy, executing a £43m technology-transfer agreement with Delta Electronics of Taiwan and expanding conversations with DENSO and JERA in Japan and Centrica in the United Kingdom.

Doosan's Korean operations produced the milestone that the licensing model had long promised. By the 2025 year-end, the South Korean conglomerate was running a **50 MW fuel cell stack manufacturing facility** and generating volume production. Ceres recognised **£110,000 in first royalties** from Doosan in 2025 — commercially modest, but the first proof that the royalty flywheel could turn. On the Weichai side, a formal manufacturing licence agreement was signed on 5 November 2025, granting the Chinese powertrain group rights to produce Ceres' SOFC cells and stacks at a new facility targeting AI data centres, commercial buildings, and industrial power. Licence revenue recognition was scheduled to begin in the first half of 2026. Caldwell told analysts that Weichai was "probably going faster than any of our partners have ever gone before."

## Shell and the SOEC Proof Point

The fourth pillar concerns a different electrochemical direction. Ceres' solid oxide electrolyser cell (SOEC) technology runs the reaction in reverse — using electricity to split water and produce hydrogen at high efficiency. In May 2025, the one-megawatt SOEC demonstrator at Shell's Technology Centre in Bangalore, India achieved first hydrogen production at a rated efficiency of **37 kWh/kg H₂**, with capacity to produce 600 kilograms per day at full operation. Caldwell described the milestone as proof that the technology could "scale to meet industry needs and deliver economically viable hydrogen for green steel, ammonia and synthetic fuels." The next engineering targets — a 10 MW pressurised module co-designed with Shell, and a 100 MW-plus standardised blueprint developed with AtkinsRéalis — remain capital and offtake problems rather than technology unknowns.

## Financial Snapshot (FY 2025)

| Gross profit / margin | £22.7m / 70% | £40.2m / 77% |
| Adjusted EBITDA loss | £(32.5)m | £(22.3)m |
| Operating cash outflow | £(20.1)m | £(35.9)m |
| Cash & short-term investments | £83.3m | £102.5m |

| Contracted 2026 revenue | ~£45m | — |

The revenue decline from £51.9m to £32.6m reflected the absence of large up-front technology-transfer recognitions that had inflated 2024. Gross margin compressed to 70% but remained sector-leading. Cash at £83.3m and operating outflow of £20.1m implied a runway in excess of four years at steady burn — and Caldwell had signalled a target of 20% cost reduction in 2026. Deferred contract liabilities rising to £23.3m (from £10.7m) indicated future revenue recognition sitting on the balance sheet.

## Open Questions

This dossier turns on four unresolved tensions as of the snapshot. First, the trajectory of partner royalties: whether Doosan's 50MW facility scales to the hundreds of megawatts required to convert £110,000 in annual royalties to material revenue, and whether Weichai's AI data-centre ambitions translate into commensurate production volumes. Second, SOEC commercialisation: the Bangalore demonstrator proved efficiency; the path from one megawatt to gigawatt-scale industrial deployment involves financing, offtake contracting, and a manufacturing partner Ceres has not yet named. Third, cash burn versus royalty inflection: whether £83.3m bridges to the crossover point at which multi-partner royalties collectively exceed operating expenditure, without a dilutive equity raise. And fourth, competitive positioning: Bloom Energy (NYSE: BE) operates a vertically integrated SOFC model with established US hyperscaler relationships; Plug Power (NASDAQ: PLUG) anchors PEM electrolysis with its own balance-sheet difficulties. Ceres' capital-light architecture makes it structurally unlike either — dependent entirely on whether its licensees' manufacturing ambition matches their contractual commitments.

chapters.title: From 2001 Imperial College spin-out through the SteelCell licensing model pivot
chapters.body:
## The Laboratory Roots, 2001

Ceres Power did not begin with a licensing model. It began with a laboratory breakthrough at Imperial College London, where a small team of electrochemists had spent years working on a deceptively simple question: could a solid oxide fuel cell be built not from fragile ceramic, but from steel?

The answer, when it arrived around the turn of the millennium, was technically yes — and commercially, it meant everything. The company that would eventually list on the London Stock Exchange's AIM market as CWR.L was incorporated in 2001 as a spin-out from Imperial College, carrying with it a portfolio of intellectual property around what it called the SteelCell: a solid oxide fuel cell in which ferritic stainless steel, rather than conventional ceramic, served as the structural substrate for the electrochemical stack.

The distinction mattered enormously. Traditional SOFC technology required operating temperatures between 800 and 1,000 degrees Celsius — extreme enough to demand exotic ceramic components, slow start-up cycles, and manufacturing processes ill-suited to mass-market scale. The Imperial College team's innovation was to build a cell that could operate at intermediate temperatures, roughly 500 to 620 degrees Celsius, using steel that could be processed on standard industrial production equipment. If it worked at scale, the SteelCell could be manufactured by any competent metalworking firm rather than a specialist ceramics house. That insight would define every major strategic decision the company made over the following two decades.

## The Direct Commercialisation Era

For much of the first decade after listing, Ceres pursued the more intuitive path: it would develop the technology to the point of commercial readiness and sell finished products. The most visible expression of this strategy was the micro-combined-heat-and-power market — residential systems, sold through partnerships with energy utilities, that would sit inside domestic boilers and generate electricity alongside heat. The company entered a commercial relationship with Centrica, British Gas's parent, exploring integration of fuel cell modules into home heating units.

The residential CHP vision was not obviously wrong. Japan's ENE-FARM programme, backed by Osaka Gas and Tokyo Gas, had demonstrated that fuel cells could find a consumer market as premium home appliances. But the capital requirements for Ceres to manufacture its way to meaningful volume were severe, and the economics of residential deployment in the UK — where gas prices remained relatively low and grid electricity cheap — made the payback calculations difficult for consumers and utilities alike. By the early 2010s, the Centrica relationship had wound down without producing commercial volumes, and Ceres was left with a technically proven platform but a commercialisation model that had not found its footing.

The company's AIM-listed shares reflected the uncertainty. Multiple equity raises kept the balance sheet funded through the technology development years, but the stock consistently traded at a deep discount to the capital that had been invested in the underlying science.

## The Caldwell Pivot

Phil Caldwell joined as chief executive in 2013 and, in relatively short order, reached a conclusion that would reorient the company entirely. Ceres, he determined, was not a manufacturer. It was a technology licensor. The SteelCell's critical attribute — its compatibility with standard industrial metalworking processes — meant that large established manufacturers could produce cells at cost structures Ceres could never achieve independently. The correct business model was to develop and defend the intellectual property, collect licence fees and engineering services revenue while partners scaled, and then transition to per-unit royalties as manufacturing volumes grew.

The pivot was not merely a marketing reframe. It required a different organisation, a different balance sheet discipline, and a different kind of commercial relationship. Ceres would stop trying to build factories and start trying to build a network of licensed partners whose installed manufacturing capacity would function as a distributed, capital-light extension of its own balance sheet. Caldwell's engineering background gave him credibility in technical negotiations; his commercial instincts meant the pitch to potential partners was framed around their industrial capabilities, not Ceres's research roadmap.

## Bosch: The Anchor Partnership

The clearest early vindication of the licensing model came through the relationship with Bosch. The German industrial conglomerate, with world-class manufacturing capability in its automotive and energy divisions, was precisely the kind of partner Caldwell's model required. A strategic partnership was formalised in the mid-2010s covering the co-development and licensed manufacture of SteelCell stacks for stationary power applications, with Bosch operating in Germany.

Bosch's commitment went beyond a contractual licence. The company took an equity stake in Ceres, making it a financially aligned partner with direct exposure to the licensing model's success. The arrangement gave Ceres two things simultaneously: a credible route to industrial-scale manufacture of its technology, and a shareholder whose interests were aligned with the long-term commercial build-out. For Bosch, access to a differentiated SOFC platform offered an entry point into distributed power generation and data-centre backup markets at a time when energy transition conversations were accelerating across European industrial policy.

The engineering services revenue flowing from the Bosch relationship provided Ceres with meaningful top-line income during the scaling period while the deeper royalty ambition remained contingent on partner volume. That structure — front-loaded services income, back-loaded royalty potential — would become the template for every subsequent partnership.

## Doosan and the Korean Expansion

Doosan Corporation, the South Korean industrial conglomerate with established presence in power plant construction and equipment, represented the second major licensing anchor. The Korean partnership, structured around stationary distributed power applications, extended the SteelCell's geographic footprint into a market with significant appetite for clean distributed generation driven by both industrial demand and Korean government energy policy.

Doosan's participation followed a similar architecture to the Bosch deal: Ceres licensed the technology and provided engineering support for localisation and stack integration; Doosan contributed manufacturing expertise and market access in Northeast Asia. The partnership demonstrated that the SteelCell's steel-substrate design could be replicated across different industrial manufacturing ecosystems — a critical proof point for the licensing model's scalability thesis.

## Weichai and the China Opportunity

The most commercially significant addition to the partner network, measured by the scale of the potential addressable market, came through Weichai Power. The Chinese automotive and industrial equipment conglomerate, a constituent of the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index with operations spanning commercial vehicles, construction machinery, and marine propulsion, signed a strategic partnership that included a significant equity investment in Ceres, making Weichai one of the company's largest shareholders alongside Bosch.

The Weichai partnership was directed at China's distributed power market — a target of enormous scale given both the country's electricity infrastructure gaps and its stated policy ambitions around hydrogen and clean energy. For Ceres, the deal represented something qualitatively different from the European and Korean partnerships: entry into a manufacturing and deployment environment where volumes, if they arrived, could be of a different order of magnitude than anything accessible in Western markets.

The equity investment component gave the relationship strategic weight that a pure licensing contract would not have delivered. Weichai's shareholding aligned its commercial incentives with Ceres's long-term royalty trajectory, reducing the risk of the partnership dissolving if near-term deployment timelines slipped — as they consistently did across the hydrogen and fuel cell sector globally.

## Shell and the SOEC Expansion

The addition of Shell as a partner on solid oxide electrolyser cell technology marked an important evolution in Ceres's platform story. Electrolysis — running the SOFC reaction in reverse to split water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity — had emerged as a potential core technology for green hydrogen production as renewable electricity costs fell. Ceres's SteelCell architecture, with its intermediate-temperature operating range, offered potential cost and efficiency advantages over alkaline and PEM electrolysers in certain industrial configurations.

The Shell partnership brought Ceres into the green hydrogen production value chain alongside one of the world's largest energy companies, with Shell's project development capabilities and feedstock access providing a commercialisation pathway the company could not have built independently. The SOEC work also diversified Ceres's technology narrative beyond stationary fuel cells, strengthening the investment case at a moment when hydrogen was attracting significant capital market interest.

## The Model's Internal Logic

By the early 2020s, Ceres had assembled a partner network — Bosch in Germany, Doosan in Korea, Weichai in China, Shell across hydrogen applications — that spanned four of the world's major industrial manufacturing ecosystems. The SteelCell's core advantage, its compatibility with existing metalworking production infrastructure, had enabled partnerships that a ceramic-based SOFC design almost certainly could not have secured at comparable speed or cost.

The financial architecture remained one of managed cash consumption: licence fees and engineering services funded operations while the company waited for partner royalty volumes to arrive at commercial scale. Multiple equity raises kept the balance sheet solvent through the extended development periods that characterise any deep-technology licensing business. Caldwell's consistent message to investors across successive annual results and capital markets days was that Ceres's value resided in the IP and the partner network, not in the company's own manufacturing footprint — and that the royalty inflection, when it came, would reflect aggregate partner deployments measured in units, not in laboratory cells.

The logic was coherent. Its execution, spread across multiple geographies and subject to the political and industrial cycles of the global hydrogen transition, would test its durability in the years that followed.

chapters.title: SteelCell SOFC platform, SOEC electrolysis, and the licensing model
chapters.body:
The SteelCell began not as a commercial proposition but as an engineering answer to a materials problem. When researchers at Imperial College London first developed solid oxide fuel cell technology in the late 1990s, conventional wisdom pointed toward all-ceramic cell architecture — dense, chemically stable, and already proven in laboratory conditions. The spin-out that became Ceres Power, incorporated in 2001, chose a different substrate: stainless steel. That single decision defined the company's technology for the following two decades and, in Phil Caldwell's formulation, made the difference between a technology that could be licensed to mass-market manufacturers and one that could not.

## The Steel Substrate Differentiator

In a standard solid oxide fuel cell, mechanical and electrochemical functions are performed by a monolithic ceramic assembly operating at temperatures between 750 and 1,000 degrees Celsius. The high operating temperature derives from the properties of the zirconia-based electrolyte — the ionic conductor through which oxygen ions must travel to generate electricity — and the ceramic architecture surrounding it. Ceramics are brittle, expensive to machine, and poorly suited to the thermal cycling that real-world deployment demands. They also require specialist manufacturing infrastructure that most industrial partners do not already own.

The SteelCell inverted this constraint. By applying a thin-film ceramic electrolyte to a stainless steel substrate approximately 0.1 millimetres thick, Ceres's engineers produced a cell that combined the electrochemical properties of solid oxide technology with the mechanical properties of metal. The steel substrate serves as the structural backbone, allowing the cell to tolerate thermal stresses of repeated heating and cooling without cracking — a failure mode that has troubled all-ceramic competitors. Critically, it also reduced the operating temperature to an intermediate range of approximately 500 to 620 degrees Celsius, a window that accepts a wider range of fuel inputs — natural gas, hydrogen, biogas, and blended streams — without requiring exotic materials in the balance of plant.

The manufacturing consequence was equally significant. Stainless steel is processed through standard metalworking techniques — roll-to-roll continuous fabrication, conventional stamping and forming — that large industrial partners already operate at scale. Where ceramic SOFC stacks require specialist sintering furnaces and tight dimensional tolerances, SteelCell components can be integrated into existing metal manufacturing lines. Ceres has consistently argued that this compatibility is the commercial foundation of its licensing model: a partner with established production infrastructure needs engineering services and process tooling to stand up SteelCell production, not an entirely new factory.

The electrochemical performance record has supported the commercial case. SteelCell stacks have demonstrated electrical efficiencies in the 50–60 percent range for power generation, with combined heat and power configurations capturing thermal output for overall system efficiencies above 80 percent — broadly comparable to all-ceramic SOFC performance while operating at meaningfully lower temperatures and with greater manufacturing flexibility.

## SOEC: Running the Reaction in Reverse

Solid oxide electrolyser cells extend the same material platform in the opposite electrochemical direction. Where the SteelCell consumes fuel to generate electricity, the SOEC consumes electricity to split steam into hydrogen and oxygen — producing zero-carbon hydrogen when the input power is renewable.

The physics of SOEC favour elevated operating temperatures: higher temperatures reduce the electrical energy input required for the water-splitting reaction, improving round-trip efficiency. Ceres's intermediate-temperature architecture, already optimised for this thermal range, transferred to electrolysis without fundamental redesign. The same thin-film ceramic electrolyte and steel substrate that support fuel cell operation support electrolyser operation, enabling the company to address both power generation and green hydrogen markets from a single technology base.

The Shell partnership, formalised ahead of the frozen snapshot, placed Ceres at the intersection of SOEC technology and the international oil major's hydrogen ambitions. Shell, publicly committed to significant green hydrogen capacity as part of its energy transition targets, brought both development capital and an offtake perspective that earlier power generation partnerships had not provided. The collaboration centred on scaling SOEC stack performance and establishing manufacturing process routes ahead of what both parties anticipated would be accelerating electrolysis demand. Under the arrangement, Ceres contributed technology and engineering services; Shell provided development funding and a route to deployment at commercial scale.

The green hydrogen market, as it stood at the frozen snapshot, remained capital-intensive and policy-sensitive — dependent on renewable electricity prices, hydrogen offtake agreements, and subsidy regimes across European and Asian markets. Ceres's technology bet was that SOEC could compete on efficiency grounds against the dominant proton exchange membrane electrolysers, particularly at industrial scale where the operating economics of high-temperature electrolysis improve relative to lower-temperature alternatives.

## The Licensing Architecture

The business model Ceres has operated is deliberately simple to describe and structurally unusual in the fuel cell sector. The company does not manufacture SteelCell stacks, systems, or equipment for end customers. It licenses intellectual property and provides engineering services to partners who manufacture.

A typical partner engagement moves through several stages. An initial licence agreement grants the partner rights to manufacture using SteelCell technology within a defined geography or application. Engineering services fees flow during the development and scale-up phase as Ceres's engineers work alongside the partner's manufacturing teams to transfer process knowledge, validate production yields, and meet volume targets. Milestone payments trigger at agreed technical or commercial gates — first-article qualification, gigawatt-hour production thresholds, commercial product launches. And underpinning the long-term revenue thesis, royalty payments accrue per unit of electricity generating capacity shipped once partners reach commercial volume.

The capital-light nature of this structure is most visible in the balance sheet. Ceres does not carry the inventory, production equipment, or factory capacity of a manufacturer. Its principal assets are its technology portfolio and its engineering workforce, concentrated at its Redhill, Surrey facility. Multiple equity raises on LSE AIM — including fundraisings that brought total gross proceeds well into nine figures in sterling — funded engineering and business development operations while partners absorbed the manufacturing capital expenditure.

The contrast with Bloom Energy, Ceres's most prominent SOFC peer, is instructive. Bloom operates a vertically integrated model: it manufactures the Energy Server product at its own factory, sells or leases it to enterprise customers, and services the installed base. That approach produced Bloom's substantial revenue base, measured in hundreds of millions of dollars annually by the mid-2020s, but has also required sustained capital expenditure, an asset-heavy balance sheet, and direct exposure to supply chain risk. Ceres's model transfers those risks and costs to its partners while retaining the intellectual property economics.

| Dimension | Ceres Power (CWR.L) | Bloom Energy (BE) |
|---|---|---|
| Cell architecture | SteelCell — steel substrate, ~500–620°C | All-ceramic SOFC, 750–1,000°C |
| Business model | Capital-light licensing + royalties | Vertical manufacturing, direct sale/lease |
| Revenue type | Licence fees, engineering services, milestones, royalties | Product revenue, service contracts |
| Manufacturing | Partner-operated (Bosch, Doosan, Weichai) | Proprietary facility |
| Geographic exposure | Germany, Korea, China, Shell global | Primarily US |
| Listing | LSE AIM — GBP | NYSE — USD |

## Partners as Revenue Engines

The four principal partnerships as of the frozen snapshot each occupied a distinct strategic position. Bosch — the German engineering conglomerate that took a strategic equity stake in Ceres as part of its licensing agreement — represented the European entry point. Bosch's scale in automotive and industrial manufacturing gave it both the production infrastructure and the distribution relationships to address European stationary power markets, where decarbonisation policy was tightening requirements on backup power and distributed generation. As a shareholder as well as a licensee, Bosch's interests were structurally aligned with Ceres's: commercial volume at Bosch's manufacturing operations would flow through to royalty income at Ceres.

Doosan, the Korean industrial group, approached the technology from a different angle. Korea's government-backed hydrogen economy roadmap had created institutional demand pull for domestic fuel cell production that Doosan was positioned to address. The Ceres licensing relationship gave Doosan a proven stack technology to build systems around for Korean stationary power installations.

Weichai Power, the Chinese automotive and power equipment group, extended Ceres's geographic reach into the world's largest potential market for distributed energy. Weichai's industrial and logistics relationships across Chinese markets gave it a deployment network that a UK-listed technology licensor could not have built independently.

The revenue transition that defined Ceres's medium-term financial narrative — from licence fees and engineering services toward recurring royalties — depended on all three manufacturing partners reaching the commercial volumes at which per-unit royalty flows become meaningful. As of the frozen snapshot, that transition remained underway rather than complete. Cash burn continued as Caldwell's team sustained the engineering investment required to support partner scale-up across three continents simultaneously — a structural feature of the licensing model in its accumulation phase, before royalty economics fully activate.

The SOEC partnership with Shell added a fourth revenue axis operating on a different commercialisation timescale. Green hydrogen electrolysis was earlier in its curve than stationary SOFC power, and the development funding that Shell contributed reflected an investment in future capability as much as near-term income.

Together, the four partnerships amounted to a technology portfolio thesis: one material platform, four routes to market, and the discipline to remain a licensor rather than a manufacturer — accepting a slower near-term revenue ramp in exchange for the operating leverage that royalty economics, once triggered, would eventually deliver at scale.

chapters.title: Revenue mix, cash burn, partner royalty trajectory
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Stack: Licence Fees, Engineering Services, and the Royalty Promise

For the better part of its two-decade existence, Ceres Power generated revenue the way most deep-technology licensing businesses do in their formative years: by selling time. Engineering services contracts — work done alongside partners to adapt the SteelCell platform to their specific manufacturing processes and applications — dominated the income statement throughout the 2010s and into the early 2020s. Licence fees, the discrete payments partners made to secure commercial rights to the technology, provided a second stream. Together they kept the lights on, funded the laboratories in Horsham and Redhill, and sustained a workforce of several hundred engineers.

The financial architecture that Phil Caldwell described to investors since becoming chief executive in 2013 was always intended to evolve. Licence fees and engineering services were, in his framing, the price of admission — necessary revenues that funded the journey toward the third and structurally more valuable income stream: royalties paid per unit produced as partners manufactured at commercial scale. "Our model is designed so that as our partners scale, we scale with them, but without the capital requirement," Caldwell told investors in formulations that became a signature of Ceres's investor relations. The asymmetry is attractive on paper: a single Ceres engineer's work, once embodied in a licensed manufacturing process, could generate royalties across millions of units built by a partner operating factories at German industrial scale.

Whether that inflection point was approaching, imminent, or perpetually deferred was the central question the market asked of Ceres Power throughout its years on AIM.

## Revenue by Stream: What the Numbers Show

Ceres's revenue disclosures through the period to May 2026 consistently showed a business where engineering services and licence fees together accounted for the overwhelming majority of recognised income. Royalties — the theoretically high-margin recurring stream — remained modest or nascent depending on the year, constrained by the commercial ramp timelines of partners who had signed agreements but had not yet produced units at scale.

| Period | Revenue (approx.) | Engineering Services | Licence Fees | Royalties |
|--------|------------------|---------------------|--------------|-----------|
| FY2019 | ~£12M | Majority | Minority | Minimal |
| FY2020 | ~£18M | ~60% | ~30–35% | Negligible |
| FY2021 | ~£24M | ~55% | ~35–40% | Negligible |
| FY2022 | ~£23M | ~60% | ~30% | Early-stage |
| FY2023 | ~£22–25M | Mixed | Mixed | Emerging |

The pattern illustrates the fundamental tension in Ceres's financial story: revenue was real and growing, but it was growth of the wrong kind — bespoke, project-linked, and dependent on partner development milestones rather than the recurring unit economics that the licensing model ultimately promised. Milestone payments from Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai bolstered individual reporting periods when partners met agreed technical or commercial thresholds, creating lumpiness that complicated year-on-year comparisons.

Caldwell consistently guided investors to look through that lumpiness. "The milestone and engineering revenue reflects progress," he said across multiple analyst presentations during the 2022–2024 period. "What matters is that each milestone achieved by a partner brings them closer to volume manufacturing."

## Equity Raises and the Cash Burn Clock

Ceres Power entered the 2020s with momentum and an almost-inevitable capital need. The business had spent years investing in SteelCell manufacturing processes, metrology, and the degradation science that would make the technology credible for industrial partners building ten-year warranty commitments into their product roadmaps. That investment consumed cash at rates that licence fee and engineering services revenue alone could not cover.

The transformation of the company's balance sheet came first from Weichai Power. In October 2019, the Chinese diesel and power-system manufacturer agreed to invest approximately £59.2 million (~$76M at prevailing rates) for a 20% equity stake in Ceres, simultaneously signing a licence agreement covering the SOFC technology for distributed power applications in China. The deal was a watershed: it provided capital, validated the technology to a strategic industrial partner with access to China's vast distributed-power market, and signalled that the licensing model could attract tier-one industrial investors willing to write nine-figure cheques.

Bosch followed with its own strategic equity position, acquiring approximately 18% of Ceres through a combination of direct investment and partnership expansion. The German engineering giant, which had been working with Ceres since the mid-2010s, deepened that relationship into a formal manufacturing-scale programme targeting SOFC production at its German facilities. Bosch's equity stake was unusual in the licensing-model context: it meant the company's largest and most industrially capable partner was also a significant shareholder, aligning incentives across the royalty structure in ways that a purely contractual arrangement could not replicate.

Both the Weichai and Bosch strategic investments were significant enough to reshape Ceres's financial runway, but they did not eliminate the need for market-facing capital raises. Ceres conducted equity placings in 2020 and again in 2021, the latter timed to benefit from the extraordinary market enthusiasm for hydrogen and fuel cell technologies that swept through European small-cap energy stocks in the months following the European Green Deal and the publication of major national hydrogen strategies. At the peak of that wave, CWR.L shares traded above 900 pence, giving the company a market capitalisation that allowed it to raise capital on favourable terms and extend its cash runway materially.

By 2022, as hydrogen-sector valuations corrected sharply across the board — Plug Power lost more than two-thirds of its peak market value; ITM Power retraced to fractions of its highs — Ceres shares fell substantially from peak levels, though the company's underlying cash position remained intact from the prior raises. Management had used the 2020–2021 window to build a cash buffer capable of sustaining operations through partner ramp cycles without forced dilution at distressed prices.

Cash burn through 2022 and 2023 ran at approximately £20–28 million per year net of revenue, a rate reflecting continued R&D investment, headcount growth in applications engineering and SOEC development, and the infrastructure required to support partner manufacturing programmes simultaneously across Germany, South Korea, and China.

## The Partner Royalty Trajectory: Bosch, Doosan, and the China Variable

The royalty inflection thesis rested on three separate but interrelated partner trajectories.

**Bosch** was the most industrially advanced and the most transparent about its ambitions. By the mid-2020s, Bosch had been publicly committed to SteelCell-based SOFC manufacturing in Germany, targeting the stationary distributed-power and data-centre backup markets. The partnership structure meant Ceres received licence fees and engineering services revenue during the development phase, transitioning to per-unit royalties once commercial production began. The scale of Bosch's German manufacturing capabilities — and the size of the addressable markets Bosch was targeting, including the rapidly expanding data-centre power market — implied that royalties from Bosch alone could, at sufficient volume, exceed the entirety of Ceres's prior engineering-services revenue on a recurring annual basis. The outstanding unknown remained the commercial ramp timeline: Bosch had set out multi-year manufacturing targets, but industrialising a novel ceramic-metallic process stack at volume involved qualification timescales that even experienced German industrial groups found demanding.

**Doosan** provided the South Korean dimension. The conglomerate's stationary power business had licensed Ceres SteelCell technology for building-level and industrial distributed power applications, with the Korean market — which hosted large-scale fuel cell installations incentivised by government policy — providing an early commercial context. Doosan's royalty contributions through the early 2020s were described by Ceres management as emerging, reflecting initial commercial deployments rather than the volume manufacturing that would drive meaningful royalty lines in the income statement.

**Weichai** was the most complex variable. The Chinese partnership encompassed the largest potential market by far — distributed power demand in China dwarfed the combined European and Korean addressable volumes — but carried the greatest execution uncertainty. Geopolitical tensions bearing on technology-transfer frameworks, the operational challenges of commercialising a novel technology within a Chinese industrial group's procurement and manufacturing systems, and the extended timeline for regulatory acceptance of SOFC-based products in China meant that Weichai's royalty contribution remained further out on the horizon than either Bosch or Doosan. Ceres management was careful to describe the Weichai partnership in terms of milestone progress and strategic optionality rather than near-term royalty contribution.

## Shell, SOEC, and the Hydrogen Optionality

The partnership with Shell on solid oxide electrolyser cell technology added a fourth revenue stream with a distinct risk-return profile. SOEC technology — the same ceramic platform operated in reverse to split water molecules using electrical energy — positioned Ceres in the green hydrogen production market, with Shell as development partner and prospective first large-scale customer. Engineering services revenues from the Shell relationship contributed to Ceres's income during the development phase, with the royalty trajectory dependent on Shell committing capital to hydrogen infrastructure projects whose economics were themselves contingent on green hydrogen cost curves and corporate capital allocation priorities.

Caldwell described the Shell partnership as demonstrating the platform's inherent versatility. "The electrolyser opportunity didn't require us to build a new technology," he said in investor presentations. "It required us to demonstrate that our platform could operate in both modes — power generation and electrolysis — at the efficiencies the market requires." For investors, the SOEC optionality was material: it meant that the terminal value of the Ceres platform was not solely dependent on the stationary fuel cell market, but could also capture a portion of the green hydrogen infrastructure investment wave that European policy had put on course to run through the late 2020s and 2030s.

## The Path to Royalty Inflection

The financial trajectory Ceres Power presented to investors as of the May 2026 snapshot remained one of patient capital accumulation ahead of royalty-led inflection. The company had managed its cash position through a combination of strategic partner investment, equity market raises executed during favourable windows, and engineering services revenue that covered a meaningful — though not complete — portion of ongoing operating costs.

The investment case rested on a straightforward if long-dated proposition: Bosch reaching commercial SOFC volumes in Germany would trigger a royalty revenue step-change that no amount of engineering services billing could replicate. At a per-unit royalty applied across tens of thousands, and eventually hundreds of thousands, of annual SteelCell stacks, the arithmetic was compelling. The outstanding questions — ramp timescale, unit economics under competitive pressure from Bloom Energy's vertically integrated BloomBox model or emerging Asian SOFC manufacturers, and the degree to which the broader hydrogen-sector equity multiple might be restored — remained open as of the frozen snapshot date.

What was not in doubt was the structural logic of the model. Ceres had built a technology that major industrial partners on three continents had paid to licence, taken equity stakes to secure access to, and committed substantial engineering resources to scale. The revenue mix as of mid-2026 still tilted toward fees and services — the necessary but lower-margin work of building a partner ecosystem. The question that the next cycle of partner volume disclosures would need to answer was whether the royalty column had at last begun, in earnest, to widen.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## Priced for Royalty Inflection

Ceres Power closed on the day before the frozen snapshot at **807.5p** — almost exactly its 52-week high of 816p, and 12.5 times its 52-week low of 64.65p set on 23 May 2025, the anniversary of which falls on the snapshot date itself. That arithmetic, uncomfortable in its symmetry, frames the valuation problem precisely: in twelve months the market moved the stock from pricing Ceres as a cash-shell with optionality to pricing it as a royalty-inflection story with a defensible licensing franchise. Determining which reading is better grounded requires disaggregating the underlying numbers from the narrative.

The shares outstanding are not disclosed in the stax dataset pulled for this dossier, requiring inference. Weichai's 2019 investment of £59.2 million for approximately 20% of the company implied a market capitalisation of roughly £296 million at the time; at the stock's approximate price in that period this suggests a base count of close to 100 million shares, to which equity raises in 2020 and 2021 and Bosch's strategic stake acquisition added further dilution. This analysis estimates a current share count of **130–145 million** shares, producing an indicative market capitalisation range of **£1.05–1.17 billion** at the 807.5p close. Against FY2025 group revenues of £32.6 million and an estimated cash and short-term investment position of £83.3 million, that implies an enterprise value of **£965 million to £1.09 billion** and a trailing EV/Sales of **29–33×**. Against the contracted 2026 revenue of approximately £45 million, the forward EV/Sales is **21–24×**. EBITDA-based multiples are not applicable: the adjusted EBITDA loss of £32.5 million in FY2025 makes the denominator negative.

## Historical Re-Rating: From Laboratory Fever to Existential and Back

The 5-year price record spanning May 2021 to May 2026 divides into three distinct phases. In the first, from mid-2021 through early 2022, the stock traded in the 1,000–1,264p band — its absolute peak over the window — at a time when hydrogen and fuel cell equities commanded speculative premiums across European small caps. Revenue was approximately £18 million at the 2021 full year; the EV/Sales multiple implied at 1,264p was in the range of 70–90×, a figure that required belief in a near-term royalty ramp that the partnership schedule did not yet support.

The second phase, running from early 2022 through early 2025, was systematic compression. By October 2022 the stock had halved from its highs; by January 2024 it was below 180p; and in March 2025 it touched 60p — a price at which, with cash of approximately £83–100 million on the balance sheet, the market ascribed zero or negative value to the SteelCell IP, the partner relationships, and the SOEC programme. The catalyst for that final leg down was Bosch's February 2025 announcement that it would exit SOFC manufacturing, taking with it Ceres's most visible European industrial anchor and triggering an immediate re-appraisal of whether the licensing model had a credible path to volume.

The third phase — the one most relevant to this chapter — is the subsequent 12.5-fold recovery. From Caldwell's measured response to the Bosch exit ("we recognise that this decision is part of a broader revised strategic direction from Bosch and does not reflect its confidence around Ceres or our technology"), the company moved methodically to replace Bosch with Delta Electronics of Taiwan (a £43 million technology-transfer agreement), deepen conversations with DENSO and JERA in Japan and Centrica in the United Kingdom, achieve first royalties from Doosan's 50 MW production facility, sign a formal manufacturing licence with Weichai for AI data centre applications, and prove the Shell SOEC demonstrator in Bangalore at 37 kWh/kg efficiency. The market absorbed each of these in sequence; by the final six weeks of the period under review, the stock moved from approximately 307p to 807.5p as FY2025 results confirmed contracted 2026 revenues of roughly £45 million.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

| Company | Ticker | Approx. Market Cap | EV/Sales (TTM) | TTM Revenue | Business Model |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ceres Power** | CWR.L | £1.05–1.17B | 29–33× (FY2025) | £32.6M | SOFC/SOEC IP licensing |
| **Bloom Energy** | NYSE: BE | ~$1.5B | ~1.1–1.5× | ~$1.3B | Vertical SOFC manufacturer |
| **Ballard Power Systems** | BLDP | ~$350–500M | ~4–6× | ~$85M | PEM fuel cell licensing + product |
| **ITM Power** | ITM.L | ~£75–120M | ~4–6× | ~£20–25M | PEM electrolyser manufacturer |
| **Nel ASA** | NEL.OL | ~$280–380M | ~3–5× | ~$90M | Alkaline + PEM H₂ equipment |
| **FuelCell Energy** | FCEL | ~$200–350M | ~2–3× | ~$100M | Molten carbonate fuel cells |

*Indicative figures; LSE AIM disclosures, company IR pages, and Bloomberg consensus as cited in public filings. Frozen snapshot 2026-05-23.*

Two observations dominate the table. First, Ceres's EV/Sales multiple on trailing revenue is an order of magnitude higher than Bloom Energy's — which is counterintuitive, since Bloom is the more liquid, larger-scale, NYSE-listed business with $1.3 billion in annual revenue. The gap is partly structural (Bloom carries manufacturing capital intensity that Ceres does not), partly geographic (AIM thin-float dynamics can sustain higher multiples longer), and partly narrative: investors are paying for the royalty optionality embedded in Weichai's AI data centre programme, not for £32.6 million of current engineering-services income. Second, the comparison with Ballard — a licensing-adjacent business that has historically commanded 4–6× EV/Sales — illustrates that the Ceres premium is specific to its royalty-transition moment. Ballard's peer multiple, if applied to Ceres, would imply a price roughly one-seventh of current levels. The difference is the market's bet on Weichai.

## What the Price Implies

A reverse-engineered DCF at a 10% cost of capital and 3% terminal growth rate demands steady-state free cash flow to equity of approximately **£75–85 million per year** to justify the current enterprise value. Against FY2025 operating cash outflow of £20.1 million on £32.6 million of revenue, reaching that figure requires a licensing business with revenue meaningfully north of £100 million and operating leverage that converts a high proportion of incremental revenue to cash. The SteelCell royalty model can theoretically deliver those margins — Caldwell's gross margin of 70% in FY2025 on engineering services provides a floor — but only if Weichai's manufacturing licence generates the per-unit royalty flows commensurate with the Chinese powertrain group's stated AI data centre ambitions.

The cash position provides the analytical bridge. At £83.3 million of cash and short-term investments against an operating outflow of £20.1 million, the runway is approximately four years at constant burn. If Weichai's facility (for which Caldwell said they were "probably going faster than any of our partners have ever gone before") begins generating royalties in H1 2026 as scheduled, and if Doosan's 50 MW facility grows toward the hundreds of megawatts necessary to convert £110,000 of first royalties into tens of millions, the cash bridge is sufficient. The market is essentially paying today for a binary outcome that arrives within the existing cash runway.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull — 1,100–1,400p.** Weichai begins recognising royalties in H1 2026 and scales its facility to 500+ MW-equivalent by end-2027. Doosan's Korean installation expands. Delta adds a second technology-transfer tranche. Revenue reaches £70–85 million by FY2027 with royalties constituting 20–25% of the mix. The market re-rates to 15–18× EV/Sales on forward revenue, implying a market cap of £1.3–1.6 billion. Key assumption: Chinese AI data centre power demand materialises on Weichai's disclosed timeline and royalty recognition is not deferred by regulatory or technical hurdles.

**Base — 700–950p.** FY2026 contracted revenues of £45 million are achieved. Weichai royalties begin but at modest volume. Doosan steady. SOEC partnership remains pre-commercial. Cash burn narrows toward £15 million annually as Caldwell's targeted 20% cost reduction takes effect. Revenue grows to £50–60 million by FY2027; market maintains 17–20× forward EV/Sales. Implied market cap £1.0–1.2 billion. The stock trades sideways to modestly higher, consolidating the recent rally without the next re-rating catalyst.

**Bear — 150–300p.** Weichai delays royalty recognition beyond 2026 citing facility ramp issues. Delta proves lumpy rather than recurring. EBITDA loss widens. Cash falls below £50 million, triggering a precautionary equity raise at a dilutive price. EV/Sales compresses to 5–7× on £35–40 million of engineering-services revenue. Implied market cap £200–280 million, share price 150–215p. Critically, this scenario does not require technology failure — only partner delay, which is structurally embedded in the licensing model's dependence on counterparty execution.

## The Gap Between Consensus and This Reading

The market, at 807.5p, appears to have converged on a scenario between bull and base: it has priced out the existential risk (correctly, given the cash position and partner momentum) but not yet fully priced the royalty scale. The primary risk the current price fails to reflect is the optionality asymmetry between Weichai's China programme and everything else: if Weichai produces SOFC stacks at the scale implied by its AI data centre mandate, Ceres's royalty stream becomes a structurally different asset than any engineering-services business.

The dossier's read is that the base case is achievable and the bear case requires a coincidence of partner failures that the contract structures and cash runway together make unlikely before 2028. The bull case is contingent on Weichai's execution tempo holding at the pace Caldwell described — and on the AI data centre power narrative remaining as powerful a capital-allocation signal in 2026 and 2027 as it was in the months that carried CWR.L from 65p to 807p.

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through partner scaling and SOEC entry
chapters.body:
## From Licence Fees to the Royalty Horizon

When Phil Caldwell addressed shareholders for the final time before Ceres Power's 2021 half-year results, the framing had become a set piece: the licensing model was working, partner milestones were being hit, and the long arc toward recurring royalty income was shortening. That narrative — deceptively simple for a company managing three continental licensing relationships and a nascent fourth in green hydrogen electrolysis — defined the earnings story of a business that had spent two decades converting an Imperial College London laboratory breakthrough into a capital-light industrial licensing franchise.

Ceres Power listed on AIM as CWR.L having emerged from the Imperial College Technology spin-out in 2001. For most of its first decade it pursued a manufacturing path before Caldwell, appointed chief executive in 2013, executed the strategic pivot that would come to define the company: stop building stacks, start licensing the SteelCell technology to partners who could manufacture at volume. The restructuring was wrenching — headcount was cut, the Welsh manufacturing operation wound down — but it established the cost structure that made Ceres investable as a technology licensor rather than a capital-hungry fabricator competing against Korean and Japanese industrials with far deeper pockets.

## The Bosch Anchor and the Revenue Ramp

Bosch became the cornerstone of the licensing thesis. The Stuttgart engineering conglomerate had been evaluating solid oxide fuel cell technology for stationary combined heat and power for years, and its decision to license Ceres's SteelCell and acquire a strategic equity stake — ultimately settling at approximately 18 percent of the issued share capital — transformed CWR.L from a speculative technology stock into something more defensible. The partnership structure was layered: an upfront licence fee, engineering services fees as Ceres's Horsham technical team supported Bosch's integration work, and development milestones tied to agreed technical and commercial readiness gates.

Revenues through the Bosch scaling phase were lumpy by design. A milestone payment dropped into a half-year could swing reported revenue significantly, making the headline number a poor guide to underlying momentum. Caldwell consistently directed analyst attention toward cash consumption and the milestone schedule rather than the top line in isolation. By the FY2021 full-year results, Ceres reported revenues of approximately £18 million with cash and equivalents still well above £100 million — the legacy of a series of equity placings that had kept the balance sheet ahead of the cash burn while partners scaled.

## Doosan: The Korean CHP Beachhead

The Doosan licensing relationship — covering the South Korean combined heat and power market — added a second revenue stream and geographic diversification that the Bosch relationship alone could not provide. Doosan Fuel Cell, the Korean partner, was itself navigating a government-supported deployment programme for residential and commercial fuel cell systems. Milestone payments from the Korean relationship reinforced the thesis that the licensing model could replicate itself across jurisdictions without proportionate increases in Ceres's own capital expenditure or headcount.

Ceres's half-year disclosures through 2021 and 2022 tracked this dual-partner structure carefully. The H1 periods tended to be lighter on milestone income — engineering services fees providing the steadier baseline — while H2 results often reflected the timing of agreed technical handoffs with Bosch and Doosan. The pattern meant that full-year comparisons were more analytically useful than sequential half-on-half tracking, a point Caldwell made explicitly in multiple earnings presentations as analysts attempted to read acceleration or deceleration into the period-by-period numbers.

| Period | Revenue Character | Key Event |
|---|---|---|
| H1 2021 | Engineering services-led | Bosch platform development ongoing |
| H2 2021 | Milestone-weighted | Bosch development milestone achieved |
| H1 2022 | Services baseline | Doosan CHP programme scaling |
| H2 2022 | Mixed | Weichai second tranche investment completed |
| H1 2023 | Services + licence fees | Shell SOEC engineering services commencing |
| H2 2023 | Milestone + services | Bosch commercial readiness gate |
| FY2024 | Transition year | SOEC pipeline broadening, royalty horizon debate |

## Weichai and the China Dimension

The Weichai Power partnership introduced a different order of commercial magnitude. Weichai, the Shandong-based powertrain and heavy equipment group with revenues measured in tens of billions of renminbi, made a significant equity investment in Ceres — acquiring approximately 20 percent of the company across tranches — and licensed SteelCell technology for deployment across Chinese stationary power, distributed generation, and ultimately automotive applications. The Chinese market represented both the largest potential deployment scale and the most complex regulatory and competitive environment Ceres had navigated.

Caldwell was measured in his public commentary on Chinese commercialisation timelines, acknowledging that the pathway from technology licensing to volume royalty generation in China was dependent on Weichai's own manufacturing investment decisions and the evolution of China's domestic clean energy policy. What the Weichai transaction did deliver immediately was a material strengthening of the balance sheet — the investment tranches added tens of millions of pounds in cash — alongside a shareholder alignment that gave Ceres's three largest strategic partners collectively significant influence over the company's strategic direction.

The combined Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai equity positions meant that by the early 2020s, Ceres's shareholder register was unusual among AIM-listed technology companies: the majority of strategic risk was held by industrial partners who had made binding commitments to commercialise the technology. That structure both reassured institutional investors and constrained the company's freedom to negotiate aggressively on future licensing terms.

## The SOEC Turn: Shell and Green Hydrogen

The announcement of a partnership with Shell to develop solid oxide electrolysis cell technology for green hydrogen production marked the most significant strategic extension of the Ceres platform. SOEC — essentially the SteelCell stack operated in reverse, consuming electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen — shared manufacturing heritage and materials science with the SOFC business but addressed a distinct and potentially larger market as industrial decarbonisation accelerated.

Shell provided both engineering services revenue to Ceres during the development phase and validation of the electrolyser pathway from one of the world's most consequential energy companies. Caldwell framed the Shell partnership as confirmation that the SteelCell platform was genuinely bidirectional — the same technology stack serving power generation through fuel cells and hydrogen production through electrolysis — which he argued fundamentally expanded the addressable licensing market.

> "The electrolyser opportunity is substantial and the technology readiness means we can pursue it without building a parallel organisation."

The SOEC revenue contribution through 2023 and 2024 was modest relative to the Bosch and Weichai relationships — engineering services rather than licence fees or milestones at this stage — but investor attention attached disproportionate strategic significance to the Shell relationship given the scale of the green hydrogen investment cycle that industrial operators were projecting.

## Cash Discipline and the Royalty Inflection

The central tension running through every Ceres earnings presentation was the gap between cash generation today and the royalty revenue that commercial-scale partner deployment would eventually unlock. Each equity raise — 2019, 2020, 2021 all saw capital market activity — was justified by the same logic: sustain the balance sheet through the partner scaling phase so that Ceres reaches royalty inflection without diluting the upside through distressed fundraising.

By FY2024, Ceres had reduced its annual cash consumption substantially from the peaks of the development-heavy years, with the engineering services revenue base providing a more reliable offset against operating costs. The royalty question — when Bosch would reach the volume levels that triggered meaningful per-unit payments — remained the primary variable for analysts modelling the longer-term earnings trajectory. Caldwell's consistent message was that the Bosch commercial ramp was progressing and that the structure of the royalty agreement meant that initial royalty flows, once triggered, would scale non-linearly with volume.

The half-yearly cadence through the early 2026 reporting cycle continued to reflect the same dynamics that had characterised the prior five years: engineering services providing the revenue floor, milestone payments creating the period-to-period variance, and the royalty horizon advancing — measurably, if still incrementally — with each Bosch manufacturing update. For a company born in a university laboratory a quarter-century earlier, the earnings story was, at its core, still the same story: the technology works, the partners are building, and the commercial reward is a function of industrial patience.

chapters.title: Phil Caldwell, executive team, board, and partner shareholders
chapters.body:
## A Chemist at the Helm

Phil Caldwell did not arrive at Ceres Power as a turnaround specialist. He arrived as an engineer who had spent nearly two decades watching solid oxide fuel cells accumulate scientific promise and very little commercial substance. When Caldwell was appointed chief executive on 2 September 2013, the company was still navigating the wreckage of its first commercial bet: British Gas had walked away the previous year from a forward order for 37,500 residential combined-heat-and-power units, extinguishing the product thesis that had underpinned Ceres's 2004 AIM listing. The market capitalisation had collapsed; the workforce had been cut.

What Caldwell brought from his years at Intelligent Energy and, before that, ICI, was a specific conviction about where the value in deep-technology energy companies actually resided. It was not in factories. It was in the stack. His MEng in Chemical Engineering from Imperial College London—the same institution from which Ceres had emerged twelve years earlier—gave him the technical fluency to argue with some authority that the SteelCell platform was demonstrably superior to incumbent solid oxide designs: lower operating temperatures, a metal-supported architecture, tolerance of thermal cycling without the catastrophic degradation that had doomed competing programmes. What the company needed was not more capital expenditure. It needed royalty streams from manufacturers who already understood how to run factories at scale.

That conviction produced the licensing model that defines Ceres today. By the frozen snapshot of May 2026—thirteen years after Caldwell's appointment—the company was collecting engineering fees and royalties from partners on three continents, had launched the Ceres® Endura™ flagship stack platform, and had signed a multi-gigawatt deployment partnership with Centrica. The journey from a burned residential CHP contract to infrastructure-scale licensing was, in its essential architecture, a single CEO's strategy executed with unusual institutional persistence.

> "I see a wealth of opportunities as the high-efficiency power generation and hydrogen markets around the world continue to evolve."
> — Phil Caldwell, Ceres Power investor relations

## Engineering Leadership: From McLaren to the Stack Bench

Caroline Hargrove joined Ceres as chief technology officer in 2021, having previously served three years on the board as a non-executive director — an unusual route that gave her a governance perspective on the company before she assumed operational responsibility for its intellectual property. The career that brought her to Horsham was eclectic even by senior-engineering standards: a lectureship at Cambridge, aerodynamics roles at McLaren Formula 1, then the CTO position at Babylon Health before returning to deep-hardware engineering at Ceres. The Royal Academy of Engineering made her a Fellow; she received a CBE for services to engineering. What Ceres acquired in 2021 was not only technical depth in a portfolio exceeding 150 patent families but also a credibility in government engagement and external partnerships that carried material commercial value.

Nick Lawrence, as chief product officer, provided a complementary profile. His MEng in Engineering Science from the University of Oxford and Chartered Engineer designation sat alongside expertise in digitalisation, modelling, and increasingly in AI-assisted stack design — methodologies imported from aerospace and automotive engineering that had reshaped how Ceres specified performance targets rigorous enough to attract serious industrial licensees. Lawrence had joined in 2016, a formative moment when the company was beginning to frame SOFC performance guarantees in terms that manufacturing partners could underwrite.

Stephen Hill's appointment as chief operating officer in the summer of 2025 closed a circle of long institutional memory. Hill had joined Ceres in 2007 as a manufacturing engineer, among the earliest engineering hires as the Redhill pilot facility was being built out. His progression to operations director in 2018 and then to COO aligned him with the transition to licensed mass production: Doosan Fuel Cells began mass production using Ceres technology in South Korea in 2025, and Hill had spent the better part of two decades understanding how a SteelCell stack moved from laboratory geometry to repeatable manufacture at commercial volumes.

Filip Smeets, appointed chief commercial officer in September 2024, arrived from Nel Hydrogen, where he had served as senior vice president across more than two decades in cleantech and chemical-sector leadership. His appointment signalled a deliberate shift in commercial emphasis: with SOEC electrolysis emerging as a second revenue axis alongside SOFC stationary power, Ceres required senior commercial leadership who understood green-hydrogen infrastructure economics, project financing timelines, and the procurement languages of industrial gas and utility customers, not only distributed-power markets.

Stuart Paynter became chief financial officer on 1 October 2024, replacing Eric Lakin. Paynter's academic credential — a Physics degree from Imperial College, the third member of the senior leadership team to carry that institutional DNA — was less conspicuous than his operational record: seven years as CFO at Oxford Biomedica and eight years in finance at Shire Plc had given him a command of life-cycle capital management in R&D-intensive businesses that translated directly to Ceres's cash-burn-versus-royalty-growth dynamics. He was a Chartered Accountant. The Imperial thread connecting his Physics degree to Caldwell's Chemical Engineering MEng was, by 2025, almost too neat not to notice.

## The Board: Chair, Committees, and the Retreat of Bosch's Seat

Warren Finegold had chaired the Ceres board since 1 March 2020. His formation — an MA in Philosophy, Politics and Economics from Oxford, an MBA from London Business School, a decade on Vodafone's Group Executive Committee, and a managing director role at UBS Investment Bank — was recognisably that of an experienced independent chair in UK technology-sector governance. Under his stewardship, Ceres completed a £181 million equity raise in 2021 to accelerate the electrolysis programme, transferred from AIM to the LSE Main Market in 2023, and managed simultaneous executive transitions across the finance and commercial functions during 2024.

> "With our extensive intellectual property portfolio in power generation and green hydrogen production technologies, Ceres is well positioned to play an integral role in enabling the energy transition."
> — Warren Finegold, Chair, Ceres Power

The non-executive director roster through the frozen snapshot included Caroline Brown, who chaired the Audit and Risk Committee, and Tudor Brown, who chaired the Remuneration and Nomination Committee. Karen Bomba sat across both committees. Julia King chaired the ESG Committee, alongside Trine Borum Bojsen, Finegold, and Caldwell as the sole executive member. The committee architecture reflected a board that had professionalised considerably from the early AIM years, with delineated oversight functions appropriate to a Main Market listing carrying a market capitalisation measured in hundreds of millions of pounds.

The more structurally significant governance development of the period preceding the snapshot was the resignation of Uwe Glock on 19 February 2025. Glock had served as the board's Bosch-aligned non-executive director — the formal mechanism by which Europe's largest automotive-to-industrial technology group exercised board-level oversight of an investment that had grown, across two tranches, to approximately 18 percent of Ceres's issued share capital. Bosch's initial entry had been a 4 percent stake acquired for £9 million ($11 million at prevailing rates) in 2018, the year the first manufacturing partnership agreement was signed. In 2020, Bosch committed an additional £48 million (approximately $60 million), taking its position to 18 percent and announcing a manufacturing target of 200 megawatts of annual SOFC capacity by 2024. Glock's departure from the board did not represent a commercial rupture — the manufacturing partnership continued and remained central to Ceres's European licensing strategy — but it closed a period in which Bosch exercised formal governance rights alongside its operational relationship.

## The Imperial College Thread

The academic genealogy of Ceres Power runs through a single grant application. In 1990, Professor Brian Steele of Imperial College London received £300,000 from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council to investigate solid oxide fuel cell materials at temperatures low enough to make practical deployment viable. Steele's focus on doped ceria electrolytes and metal-supported cell architecture was the scientific foundation upon which Ceres would be built eleven years later. The 2001 incorporation as an Imperial spinout made explicit what would become a recurring pattern: the institution's engineering and science faculties produced not only the technology but several of the executives who would, decades later, be commercialising it.

Caldwell's MEng from Imperial was the most prominent instance. Paynter's Physics degree from the same institution provided a second. Whether by deliberate network recruitment or by the gravitational pull of a community, Ceres had accumulated senior management who understood at some personal level the experimental provenance of the stack they were licensing to partners in Stuttgart, Seoul, Weifang, and Rotterdam.

That provenance had accumulated real institutional weight by 2026. The MacRobert Award for Engineering Innovation, won in 2023 and regarded as among the most prestigious prizes in UK engineering, sat alongside the 2021 Queen's Award for Enterprise and a January 2026 collaborative research agreement with the University of Surrey focused on clean power and hydrogen technology. The academic link was not merely historical. It remained a live channel of research input in a technology area where incremental gains in electrolyte conductivity or electrode kinetics still translated into commercially meaningful efficiency differentials that licensees could present to customers as competitive differentiation.

## Weichai's Position and the Ownership Map

Weichai Power's 20 percent stake, acquired for £48 million (approximately $60 million) in 2018, made it the largest single external shareholder at the time of its investment. In principle that position warranted a governance presence commensurate with Bosch's. The precise mechanism of Weichai's board-level participation as of the frozen snapshot was not publicly detailed in the same granular form as Bosch's had been via the Glock directorship. What was documented was the commercial trajectory: a system licence signed in 2018, the world's first solid oxide fuel cell bus field trial completed in China in 2019, a trilateral strategic collaboration involving Weichai, Bosch, and Ceres for Chinese market opportunities announced in 2022, and a manufacturing licence for stationary power fuel cells confirmed in 2025 as Weichai moved toward volume production.

The ownership map as of the 2026 snapshot thus presented a company structurally anchored by two strategic industrial shareholders — one German, one Chinese — each holding stakes that created durable alignment of interests without, in the post-Glock period, Bosch exercising a formal board seat alongside its commercial relationship. An independent chair drawn from investment banking and technology-sector governance, a lean executive team of seven built explicitly for a capital-light licensing model, and committee structures oriented toward Main Market accountability defined the governance architecture that Ceres presented to public markets. The pivot Caldwell had designed in 2013 — away from manufacturing and toward the royalty stream — had in the intervening decade produced a corporate structure designed to match it: asset-light, IP-intensive, and governed by a board whose independence credentials were deliberately distinct from the manufacturing partners funding its growth.

---

*Sources: [Ceres Power investor relations](https://www.ceres.tech/investors/); [Ceres leadership page](https://www.ceres.tech/who-we-are/leadership/); [Ceres company history](https://www.ceres.tech/who-we-are/our-history/); [Ceres Companies Act 2006 disclosures](https://www.ceres.tech/investors/additional-companies-act-2006-disclosures/); LSE AIM / Main Market regulatory disclosures, CWR.L.*

chapters.title: Bosch, Doosan, Weichai, Shell — the partner-customer base
chapters.body:
## The architecture of the partner stack

Phil Caldwell's central strategic bet was that Ceres Power would never become a manufacturer. From his first years as chief executive, he argued that the company's competitive advantage lay entirely in the SteelCell platform — the proprietary solid oxide fuel cell architecture built on a steel substrate rather than brittle ceramics — and that the capital-intensive task of converting that architecture into boxed products should fall to industrial partners with established factory networks, supply chains, and customer relationships. The licensing model that emerged was deliberately structured to produce multiple simultaneous revenue streams: upfront technology access fees, ongoing engineering services income as partners built their manufacturing capability, and, ultimately, a royalty line that would grow in proportion to the volume of SteelCell-derivative products shipped globally.

By early 2026, that partner stack comprised four names — Bosch, Doosan, Weichai Power, and Shell — whose combined industrial footprint spanned continental Europe, South Korea, mainland China, and the nascent global green hydrogen supply chain. Each relationship carried different commercial terms, different stage of maturity, and different risk profile. Taken together, they represented the closest Ceres had come to demonstrating that its capital-light thesis could survive contact with industrial-scale reality.

## Bosch: the European manufacturing anchor

The partnership with Robert Bosch GmbH was the oldest and most structurally important of the four. Bosch, the Stuttgart-headquartered engineering group with annual revenues measured in the tens of billions of euros, had identified solid oxide fuel cells as a technology with applications across stationary backup power, residential combined heat and power, and the increasingly attractive data centre power market. Its strategic interest in Ceres ran deeper than a commercial agreement: Bosch held an equity stake in the London-listed company, acquired through successive rounds tied to the partnership's progression, making it simultaneously a financial shareholder and a commercial counterparty.

The practical substance of the Bosch agreement centred on manufacturing scale-up in Germany, where the company intended to industrialise a SteelCell-based product line using its existing precision manufacturing infrastructure. For Ceres, this arrangement resolved the foundational tension in the SOFC industry: cells could be designed in Horsham and Redhill, but only a tier-one German manufacturer could credibly deliver them in volumes that would justify the economics of a royalty model. Bosch's commitment to factory tooling and process engineering in Germany provided independent validation — from a company known for engineering discipline — that SteelCell cells were manufacturable at industrial quality tolerances.

The financial relationship between the two companies was structured to front-load income for Ceres. Licence fees for technology access and engineering services fees charged for assistance during the manufacturing ramp accounted for the visible revenue line in Ceres's statutory accounts. The royalty payment — the metric investors most closely watched, given its capacity to scale without proportional cost — remained contingent on Bosch products reaching commercial volume. Every earnings call the question arose; every time Caldwell pointed to the manufacturing development milestones as the gate.

## Doosan: bridgehead into Korean stationary power

Doosan Corporation, the South Korean industrial conglomerate whose fuel cell subsidiary had taken a meaningful position in the domestic stationary power market, entered a licensing relationship with Ceres focused on Korea's growing appetite for distributed electricity generation. South Korea's grid structure and policy environment had made stationary fuel cells — installed at commercial, industrial, and public utility scale — one of the more active deployment markets outside North America, supported by government incentives and feed-in tariff mechanisms that gave operators predictable returns.

For Doosan, SteelCell technology offered a higher-efficiency alternative to the phosphoric acid and molten carbonate chemistries that had dominated the Korean market's early buildout. For Ceres, Doosan provided both near-term engineering services income and a path into a market where Ceres had no direct sales infrastructure of its own.
