The partnership mirrored the Bosch structure in its mechanics — Ceres licensing the technology, providing engineering support during product development, and standing to receive royalties as Doosan products moved into the field — but operated in a distinct regulatory and procurement context, where government-linked utilities and chaebol-affiliated project developers were the effective end customers.

Doosan Fuel Cell's own position as a separately-capitalised entity within the broader Doosan group added a layer of structural transparency: its project pipeline and delivery volumes were visible through its own Korean market disclosures, giving Ceres investors a secondary source of data on the commercial traction of the technology Ceres had licensed.

## Weichai: the Chinese bet

The most financially substantial single transaction in Ceres Power's history was Weichai Power's decision to take a significant equity stake in the company — a commitment that ran into the hundreds of millions of pounds on a sterling-denominated basis and represented one of the largest Chinese strategic investments in a British energy technology company in the years preceding the frozen snapshot. Weichai, headquartered in Weifang in Shandong province, was among China's largest manufacturers of diesel engines and drivetrain systems, with a diversification mandate that had already led it into battery electric vehicles, forklift trucks, and natural gas power systems.

The logic of the Weichai investment was geographic: China's distributed power market, spanning off-grid industrial sites, backup generation at data centres and telecommunications infrastructure, and combined heat and power applications in industrial zones, represented a scale of addressable demand that no other jurisdiction could match. A licensing relationship that worked in Germany and Korea became categorically more valuable if it could be replicated across Chinese manufacturing at Chinese volume. Weichai's factory network, logistics infrastructure, and relationships with provincial utilities and state-owned industrial customers gave Ceres a distribution capability in China that it could not have built independently.

The equity stake gave Weichai a continuing interest in Ceres's technology roadmap, creating alignment around engineering milestones rather than purely commercial ones. For Ceres, the capital raised provided runway while the partnership's engineering development work proceeded — but, more importantly, it brought credibility. A major Chinese industrial company committing balance-sheet capital to a British AIM-listed fuel cell developer carried a different message than a contractual partnership alone.

## Shell and the SOEC pivot

The partnership with Shell introduced a structurally distinct technology application to Ceres's commercial portfolio. Where the Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai relationships were centred on the fuel cell operating direction — hydrogen or natural gas in, electricity and heat out — the Shell agreement concerned solid oxide electrolyser cells, in which the same ceramic stack architecture runs in reverse: electricity in, water in, green hydrogen out.

Shell, evaluating options for industrial-scale green hydrogen production that could ultimately feed refinery operations, synthetic fuel pathways, and industrial offtake, identified high-temperature solid oxide electrolysis as a technology with thermodynamic advantages over the lower-temperature proton exchange membrane systems deployed by companies such as Plug Power. SOEC electrolysis, operating at temperatures where the electrical energy required per kilogram of hydrogen is substantially lower, offered a route to more efficient green hydrogen production provided the capital cost of the electrolyser stack could be brought down to competitive levels.

For Ceres, the partnership with Shell represented a validation of the company's contention that the SteelCell platform was genuinely bidirectional — a single technology base applicable to both power generation and electrolysis, each serving distinct commercial markets with different demand drivers. The engineering challenge of optimising cells for electrolyser duty differed from fuel cell optimisation, and the Shell partnership provided both funding and a defined industrial application context in which to conduct that development work.

## The royalty escalator and partner economics

| Partner | Geography | Application | Revenue stage (as of Q1 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bosch | Germany / Europe | SOFC stationary, data centre | Engineering services + licence fees; royalty pre-commercial |
| Doosan | South Korea | SOFC stationary utility | Engineering services + project royalties |
| Weichai Power | China | SOFC distributed power | Equity investment + early engineering services |
| Shell | Global | SOEC green hydrogen | Research and development services |

The structural logic of Ceres's partner economics was best understood as a staged escalator. In the early phases of each relationship, income comprised upfront technology licence fees — lump sums paid for the right to access and manufacture using the SteelCell architecture. As development advanced, engineering services fees dominated, compensating Ceres's teams in Horsham and Redhill for the substantial work of transferring manufacturing knowledge to a partner's factory floor. The third and most valuable stage — royalty payments indexed to shipped product volume — had not yet materialised at scale across the partner stack as of the frozen window.

That dependency on future royalty realisation remained the central tension in Ceres's investment case. The company's cash position required periodic attention, met through a combination of equity capital markets activity and partner milestone payments. The bears argued that each partnership extended the timeline before royalty-driven cash generation, and that the pattern of announced agreements had so far delivered engineering services income rather than the compounding commercial revenue the licensing model promised. The bulls pointed to the strategic equity commitments — Bosch's stake, Weichai's substantial investment — as evidence that counterparties with genuine manufacturing capability had concluded the technology would perform at scale and had committed capital accordingly.

What neither camp disputed was that Ceres had assembled a partner network of unusual quality. A German precision engineering giant, a Korean industrial fuel cell operator, a Chinese powertrain manufacturer with state-adjacent distribution, and one of the world's largest energy companies did not each commit time and capital to the same British AIM-listed technology company without independent due diligence reaching similar conclusions. The question was timing — when the engineering development phases across all four relationships would convert into the royalty income that made the licensing model self-sustaining.

chapters.title: Where Ceres sits against Bloom Energy, Plug Power, and broader fuel cell set
chapters.body:
## The Vertical Incumbent: Bloom Energy

Ceres Power's most direct technology peer was Bloom Energy (NYSE: BE), a San Jose, California company that had commercialised solid oxide fuel cell power generation at scale since its 2018 NYSE listing but had been deploying product commercially since the early 2010s. Where Ceres had built a capital-light licensing platform, Bloom had pursued the opposite strategy: deep vertical integration, proprietary manufacturing, and direct sales to corporate customers through its flagship "Energy Server" product line.

A single Bloom Energy Server — roughly the size of a shipping container — generated between 100 and 300 kilowatts of alternating current from natural gas, biogas, or hydrogen, with typical net electrical efficiency in the mid-to-upper-50 percent range at system level. At multi-megawatt installations, Bloom had emerged as a preferred baseload and backup power provider for hyperscale data centres, counting AT&T, Apple, and Samsung among long-standing anchor customers. Annual revenues reached approximately $1.33 billion in 2024, placing Bloom roughly fifteen to twenty times the revenue scale of Ceres by that measure.

The strategic contrast was stark. Bloom manufactured its own ceramic cells, stacks, modules, and balance-of-plant hardware at facilities in Delaware and Bengaluru, carrying associated capital expenditure, inventory risk, and labour exposure directly on its own balance sheet. That vertical posture allowed tight control over performance and quality — Bloom CEO K.R. Sridhar consistently argued that proprietary manufacturing was essential to the reliability guarantees underlying multi-year service contracts — but it required sustained capital markets access. The company had operated at an adjusted operating loss for most of its listed history, funding growth through equity and debt instruments before edging toward positive operating income as data-centre demand surged in 2024 and 2025.

By contrast, Ceres carried negligible capital expenditure relative to revenue. Caldwell had drawn an explicit parallel, across multiple investor day presentations, to the fabless semiconductor model: Ceres designed the intellectual property and provided the technical support; Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai brought manufacturing scale and market access.

> "We're not a manufacturer — we're a technology company. Our partners have the factories, the customer relationships, and the balance sheets to deploy at scale. We provide the platform."

Whether the fabless analogy held fully — chip IP travels across foundries more fungibly than solid oxide chemistry, and Ceres's technology was inseparable from deep co-development with each partner — was a question analysts pressed. But the cash economics differed sharply in Ceres's favour on capital intensity.

By 2025, Bloom had also entered the solid oxide electrolyser cell market with its own SOEC product, leveraging the same oxide chemistry platform it had developed for fuel cells. That move brought Bloom into direct competition with Ceres's SOEC programme and the Shell partnership — the first meaningful overlap between the two companies on the hydrogen side of the ledger.

| Metric | Ceres Power (CWR.L) | Bloom Energy (NYSE: BE) |
|---|---|---|
| Business model | IP licensing | Vertical manufacturer |
| Primary technology | SOFC + SOEC (SteelCell) | SOFC + SOEC (Energy Server) |
| Revenue (approx. FY2024) | ~£25–30M | ~$1.33B |
| Manufacturing | Partners (Bosch, Doosan, Weichai) | Proprietary (Delaware, India) |
| Listed exchange | LSE AIM | NYSE |
| Key geographies | Europe, Korea, China | North America, Korea |
| Capital expenditure posture | Capital-light (partner-funded) | Capital-intensive (self-funded) |

---

## The PEM Electrolysis Pack: Plug Power, Nel, and ITM

On the hydrogen production side, Ceres's Shell partnership positioned SteelCell SOEC technology against a different competitive set: proton exchange membrane electrolysers, which had dominated industrial green hydrogen investment through the early 2020s.

Plug Power (NASDAQ: PLUG) was the largest and most prominent PEM electrolyser and fuel cell company in the United States, having spent the decade following its commercial pivot building out hydrogen infrastructure for forklift fleets and, later, green hydrogen production sites. By 2023, Plug was generating revenues approaching $900 million annually — but at enormous operating losses that triggered a going-concern disclosure in November of that year. The company's ambition to build a national green hydrogen network in the United States had consumed capital at a pace revenues could not match. An emergency Department of Energy loan guarantee process and subsequent restructuring became the defining narrative through 2024 and into 2025, serving as a cautionary exhibit for investors assessing the commercial readiness of the broader green hydrogen sector.

PEM electrolysis carried distinct characteristics from solid oxide electrolyser technology. PEM systems operated at relatively low temperatures — typically below 80 degrees Celsius — and could ramp output rapidly, making them well-suited to absorbing intermittent renewable electricity. Their round-trip efficiency in converting electricity to hydrogen was, however, lower than the theoretical ceiling achievable with SOEC. Ceres's SteelCell electrolyser operated above 700 degrees Celsius and could exploit waste-heat co-supply to reduce the electrical energy required per kilogram of hydrogen produced — a thermodynamic advantage that translated, under favourable industrial configurations, into 20 to 30 percentage points better electrical-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency than competing PEM systems.

Nel ASA (Oslo: NEL), the Norwegian electrolyser manufacturer, offered both alkaline and PEM systems and had cultivated a broader industrial customer base than Plug, though it too had struggled to translate installed-capacity growth into profitability. ITM Power (LSE: ITM), the Sheffield-based PEM manufacturer, had undergone significant restructuring after execution difficulties at its Bessemer Park gigafactory delayed commercial scale-up; by 2025, ITM had retreated to a more conservative deployment trajectory. Both companies served as live benchmarks against which the solid oxide case for green hydrogen would need to be proven at meaningful volume — a proof that remained largely prospective at the frozen snapshot date.

---

## FuelCell Energy and the Molten Carbonate Rump

FuelCell Energy (NASDAQ: FCEL) occupied a different technological corner: molten carbonate fuel cells, a higher-temperature stationary power technology that had found industrial niche applications in carbon capture and power generation but had not achieved the commercial momentum of SOFC. Annual revenues in the range of $100 million placed FuelCell Energy in a broadly similar scale bracket to Ceres, though its technology was not directly competitive with the SteelCell platform. Both companies nonetheless competed for the same pools of industrial decarbonisation capital, government subsidy attention, and utility procurement interest — a dynamic that kept FuelCell Energy on the comparison sheet of any institutional investor building a sector position in stationary clean energy.

---

## The Licensing Model: Strategic Trade-Off in Full Relief

The competitive landscape as of May 2026 illuminated a fundamental question running through every investor conversation Ceres had: was the capital-light licensing model a durable competitive advantage or a ceiling on value capture?

The bull case rested on partner leverage. If Bosch deployed SteelCell-derived SOFC systems across European data centres and industrial sites, Weichai placed units across China's distributed power market, and Doosan served Korean commercial customers, Ceres would collect royalties on an installed base that no pure-play manufacturer of its balance-sheet size could have funded independently. The company would have converted intellectual property into a globally distributed revenue stream without building a single factory or carrying a single customer contract.

The bear case noted that partners controlled the customer relationship, the deployment pace, and the commercial pricing. Bosch could slow its SOFC programme in response to competing heat-pump priorities in the European residential market. Weichai could pivot amid Chinese industrial policy shifts. Neither event would show up in Ceres's operations until it appeared in licensing revenue, creating an information lag that made near-term forecasting inherently uncertain and placed a premium on partner relationship management that could not easily be read from public disclosures.

Bloom's trajectory offered the alternative lesson. Vertical integration had allowed Bloom to move faster in the American data-centre market than any licensed partner could have moved on Bloom's behalf, and the power-demand surge of 2024 and 2025 was a tailwind Bloom captured directly on its own income statement. Ceres captured the same secular trend only insofar as its partners elected to address it — and at the pace those partners set.

> "The licensing model means our technology can scale in ways that would be impossible if we had to fund all that manufacturing ourselves. We want our IP in as many units as possible, deployed by the best manufacturers in each market."

That framing — consistent across Caldwell's public statements at capital markets events through 2024 and 2025 — captured Ceres's self-conception accurately. Whether the public markets would ultimately reward the royalty model at the premium multiples typically applied to semiconductor IP businesses, or discount it as a proxy for execution risk sitting in partners' hands, remained the central valuation question facing Ceres Power at the frozen snapshot date. The answer depended less on the chemistry — solid oxide's efficiency credentials were not seriously contested — than on whether Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai would deploy at the volumes required to make the royalty stream large enough to matter.

chapters.title: From 2001 Imperial spin-out through partner scaling and SOEC entry
chapters.body:
## Birth in a Horsham Lab

The company that would eventually reshape how the world's largest industrial conglomerates think about distributed power generation emerged in 2001 from a cluster of materials science research at Imperial College London. Its founding proposition was deceptively simple: that solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic electrochemical devices capable of converting hydrogen or natural gas directly into electricity without combustion — could be manufactured at a cost and operating temperature low enough to cross the commercial threshold that had defeated every prior attempt.

What distinguished Ceres Power from the outset was a materials insight. Traditional SOFCs used fragile ceramic substrates that required sintering at temperatures above 1,000°C, making them expensive to fabricate and prone to thermal cracking across operating cycles. The Imperial team's breakthrough was to bond the active ceramic layers onto a thin-gauge ferritic stainless steel substrate — a process engineering choice that brought sintering temperatures down to approximately 600°C, slashed materials costs, and made the cell manufacturable on equipment already familiar to automotive suppliers. They named it the SteelCell. The branding understated the novelty; the engineering did not.

The company listed on the London Stock Exchange's AIM market under the ticker CWR.L, initially pursuing a vertically integrated model — building and selling fuel cell systems directly. Progress was slow and capital-intensive. By the early 2010s, the board recognised that attempting to out-manufacture established energy hardware companies was neither achievable nor strategically coherent for a technology-originator of Ceres's size. The pivot that followed defined the company's next decade.

## The Caldwell Doctrine

Phil Caldwell joined the board and became chief executive in 2013, inheriting a company with compelling technology, limited cash, and a business model that had failed to scale. His diagnosis was structural: Ceres could not profitably manufacture at the volumes required to drive down the cost curve, but it could license a platform technology to partners who already possessed the manufacturing infrastructure, distribution channels, and balance sheets to do so.

The licensing model Caldwell constructed was unusual in the fuel cell sector, where most competitors — most visibly Bloom Energy in the United States — remained vertically integrated, owning their manufacturing and their customer contracts. Ceres would instead collect licence fees, engineering services revenue, and ultimately volume royalties as partners reached commercial scale. The capital-light structure preserved cash. The strategic risk was dependency: Ceres's revenue trajectory became contingent on its partners' commercial execution rather than its own.

That dependency would prove both the model's greatest vulnerability and, as a portfolio of major industrial names signed on, its most compelling validation signal.

## The Partnership Architecture

The first anchor partnership of the Caldwell era came with Doosan Corporation, the South Korean conglomerate, which engaged Ceres for stationary power applications. Doosan's interest was grounded in the Korean government's long-running hydrogen economy roadmap and the conglomerate's existing fuel cell business serving commercial building and utility markets. The relationship gave Ceres its first proof point that the SteelCell platform could be transferred to an external manufacturer and that engineering services — supporting partner integration teams — could generate meaningful near-term revenue while royalty volumes built.

The more strategically consequential partnership followed with Bosch GmbH, the German industrial and automotive giant. Bosch's engagement with Ceres went beyond a licensing arrangement: the Stuttgart conglomerate took a strategic equity stake in the company, aligning incentives and signalling to the broader market that a partner of Bosch's engineering rigour had evaluated the SteelCell technology and judged it manufacturable at the volumes required for residential and commercial heat-and-power applications across continental Europe. Bosch had identified the residential combined heat and power market — micro-CHP units replacing gas boilers — as a natural application for SOFC technology, and the SteelCell's operating temperature and fuel flexibility made it compatible with Germany's existing natural gas network during the energy transition.

Simultaneous with the European partnership, Ceres secured its most geographically significant relationship: Weichai Power, the Chinese heavy-equipment and powertrain manufacturer. Weichai, which produces diesel engines, transmissions, and forklifts, had been watching the Chinese government's escalating commitment to hydrogen and fuel cell technology. Like Bosch, Weichai converted its partnership into an equity position, becoming a strategic shareholder in Ceres and bringing the prospect of manufacturing at Chinese volumes — a market whose scale dwarfs the European residential CHP segment — into the forward royalty calculus.

The three-partner structure — Doosan in Korea, Bosch in Germany, Weichai in China — gave Ceres a geographic diversification across three of the world's largest advanced manufacturing economies and three distinct applications within a single technology platform. The SteelCell was being stress-tested across Korean utility installations, German residential boiler replacements, and Chinese industrial and distributed power applications simultaneously.

## The SOEC Pivot

The company's strategic arc took a second significant turn with the announcement of a partnership with Shell on solid oxide electrolyser cell technology. SOEC is, in electrochemical terms, SOFC run in reverse: rather than consuming hydrogen to generate electricity, an electrolyser cell consumes electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The same ceramic materials chemistry that Ceres had spent two decades optimising for fuel cell applications translated directly into electrolyser cell design — a platform adjacency that most competitors lacked.

Shell's interest was in green hydrogen production at industrial scale. Where PEM electrolysers — the technology used by Plug Power and Nel ASA — operate efficiently at moderate temperatures, SOECs operate at elevated temperatures where the thermodynamics of water splitting are inherently more favourable, enabling higher efficiency when waste heat is available from industrial processes. The Shell partnership positioned Ceres inside the green hydrogen supply chain at precisely the moment that European industrial policy, accelerated by the 2022 energy crisis, was committing tens of billions of euros to domestic green hydrogen infrastructure.

## Forward Catalysts

| Catalyst | Status at frozen window | Timeline signal |
|---|---|---|
| Bosch SOFC royalty inflection | Engineering services phase; volume manufacturing scaling in Germany | Royalties contingent on residential CHP product launch volumes |
| Doosan commercial expansion | Stationary power deployments in Korea | Tied to Korean government hydrogen policy cadence |
| Weichai China volumes | Manufacturing partnership active; Chinese distributed power market | Subject to China regulatory and grid-access conditions |
| Shell SOEC scale-up | Joint development; green hydrogen policy tailwinds in Europe | Dependent on EU hydrogen infrastructure build pace |
| Additional partner licensing | Management has referenced openness to new geographies and applications | No announced deal at frozen window |

The royalty inflection Caldwell has consistently framed as the model's defining moment — the point at which partner manufacturing volumes translate engineering milestone payments into a recurring revenue stream — remained, at the frozen window of May 2026, the principal forward catalyst and the principal uncertainty. The licence fees and engineering services revenue that have sustained the company through its scaling phase are structurally bounded; the royalty line, if partners reach volume, is not. That asymmetry is the investment thesis and the risk in one.

From a 2001 steel substrate in an Imperial College laboratory to a four-partner licensing portfolio spanning Korea, Germany, China, and the global green hydrogen market, Ceres Power's quarter-century trajectory is the story of a technology that survived long enough to become the platform its founders believed it could be. Whether the royalty inflection arrives before the cash position demands another equity raise is the question its shareholders are now pricing.

chapters.title: SteelCell IP, SOEC IP, Imperial College heritage, patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## From Imperial Ceramics to Steel Substrate

The intellectual foundations of Ceres Power trace to a laboratory on Exhibition Road. In 2001, a team of materials scientists at Imperial College London spun out a company built around a deceptively simple insight: that solid oxide fuel cells did not have to be fragile ceramic wafers operating at furnace temperatures. The founding work drew directly on the electrochemistry tradition cultivated at Imperial by Professor Brian Steele, whose decades of research into fast ion conductors and mixed ionic–electronic conductors had established the college as a global centre for solid-state electrochemistry. Steele, who died in 2012, had argued that intermediate-temperature operation—around 500 to 620 degrees Celsius rather than the 800 to 1,000 degrees required by first-generation ceramic cells—would be the key to commercially viable fuel cells. His students built a company to prove it.

The vehicle was a metal substrate. By depositing the functional electrochemical layers—anode, electrolyte, cathode—onto a ferritic stainless-steel support rather than onto brittle yttria-stabilised zirconia ceramics, the founding team produced a cell that could withstand thermal cycling, tolerated modest fuel impurities, and could in principle be manufactured on existing steel-processing equipment. They called the resulting architecture the SteelCell. The name carried a double meaning: a tribute to the professor whose theoretical work it embodied, and a literal description of its distinguishing material innovation.

## Patent Portfolio: Breadth as a Licensing Asset

A licensing model lives or dies by the defensibility of its underlying intellectual property. Ceres built its patent estate with that commercial logic in mind. By the time the company had established its three major SOFC partnerships—Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai Power—its portfolio had expanded to cover not only the core metal-supported cell architecture but the electrode materials, sealant systems, interconnect designs, and stack assembly methods that together constitute a manufacturable product.

The portfolio's breadth reflected a deliberate strategy. Unlike vertically integrated competitors such as Bloom Energy, which derived competitive advantage partly from manufacturing scale, Ceres had to rely on IP exclusivity to justify its licensing fees and to give partners confidence that they were acquiring a defensible technology position. Ceres filed patents in the United Kingdom, the United States, Europe, South Korea, China, and Japan—the jurisdictions of its four principal partners—ensuring that licensees received meaningful territorial protection and that potential imitators in each region faced a patent thicket rather than an open landscape.

The SteelCell's core claim—a fuel cell on a metallic support—was supplemented over two decades by incremental innovations in cathode infiltration techniques, which improved power density; in reforming catalyst formulations, which extended fuel flexibility; and in manufacturing process controls, which were necessary to transfer the technology from Ceres's pilot line to Bosch's industrial facilities in Bamberg and Weichai's plants in Shandong. Each process innovation typically generated additional patent filings, compounding the portfolio's depth.

## The SOEC Extension

When Ceres entered its partnership with Shell on solid oxide electrolyser cells, the company effectively demonstrated that its IP estate could be turned inside out. An SOEC runs the same electrochemical reactions as an SOFC in reverse: instead of oxidising hydrogen to generate electricity, it uses electricity to split steam into hydrogen and oxygen. The ceramic and electrode materials science was closely related, but the operating conditions, degradation mechanisms, and stack management requirements differed enough to demand a new body of patents.

Ceres filed SOEC-specific intellectual property covering electrolysis stack architecture, electrode materials optimised for oxidising conditions, and system-level balance-of-plant designs suited to industrial-scale green hydrogen production. The Shell partnership provided both validation and co-development funding, with joint work conducted partly at Ceres's Redhill engineering site and partly at Shell's technology centre. The effect was to convert the Shell relationship from a straightforward customer arrangement into a collaborative IP-generating exercise, the fruits of which Ceres retained rights to license more broadly.

## Redhill: The Engineering Campus

The Ceres engineering campus in Redhill, Surrey, served as the physical expression of the company's R&D strategy. Distinct from the corporate headquarters in Horsham, Redhill housed the pilot manufacturing line, the electrochemical test rigs, the materials characterisation equipment, and the engineering teams responsible for technology transfer to partners. When Bosch or Doosan sent delegations to validate stack performance or to train their own engineers on SteelCell assembly procedures, Redhill was the destination.

Ceres invested consistently in the site. Annual research and development expenditure, partly offset by partner-funded engineering programmes, ran at levels that represented a substantial fraction of total revenue—a pattern characteristic of early-stage licensing businesses that must sustain IP generation while commercial royalties remain modest. [Ceres Power annual reports, CWR.L AIM disclosures](https://www.cerespower.com/investors/) recorded R&D costs in the tens of millions of pounds per year, with partner contributions from Bosch, Doosan, and Weichai providing material offsets that allowed the engineering headcount to grow without proportional dilution pressure on shareholders.

The Redhill pilot line performed a function that no patent filing could replicate: it demonstrated, in physical hardware, that the SteelCell could be assembled with yields and repeatability sufficient for industrial licensing. Partners arriving at Redhill could observe cells being deposited, stacks being assembled, and systems being run under load. That demonstration capability was itself a form of IP—tacit knowledge embedded in processes, tooling, and trained engineers rather than in patent claims, and therefore substantially harder for a competitor to replicate from published documents alone.

## Heritage and Differentiation

Two decades after its Imperial College spin-out, Ceres occupied a distinctive position in the solid oxide landscape. It was neither a manufacturer nor a pure research institution, but something in between: a technology custodian that generated IP, validated it at pilot scale, transferred it to industrial partners, and collected royalties on the resulting production. The SteelCell's metal substrate remained the central differentiating claim—no major competitor had successfully commercialised an equivalent architecture at comparable scale—and the Imperial College heritage lent the company academic credibility that supported both partner negotiations and investor communications. Phil Caldwell returned frequently to the founding science in public statements, framing Ceres not as a fuel cell company in the conventional sense but as the guardian of a materials science breakthrough that happened to have found its highest expression in an electrochemical device.

chapters.title: Cash burn, partner concentration, SOFC market dynamics, geopolitical, technology, governance
chapters.body:
## The Long Wait for Royalties

Ceres Power's central promise rested on a proposition that was elegant in theory and grinding in practice: license the SteelCell platform to deep-pocketed manufacturers, collect milestone payments while partners scaled, then harvest recurring royalties once commercial volumes arrived. The gap between those two phases — engineering services revenue on one side, royalty inflection on the other — defined the company's financial risk profile for most of its listed life.

Through the years following Ceres's landmark partnerships with Bosch and Doosan, the company continued to consume cash. Revenue from engineering services and licence fees covered a portion of operating costs, but not all of them. Each annual results announcement brought the same structural disclosure: net cash outflow from operations, partially offset by partner milestone receipts, partially funded by existing cash reserves. The question was not whether Ceres burned cash — it did — but whether royalty scale-up would arrive before the balance sheet required replenishment.

Phil Caldwell, who had helmed the business since 2013, consistently framed the trajectory as a compression problem rather than a structural flaw. The capital-light model meant Ceres itself did not need to build gigawatt factories; the cost was time, not steel. But time had a GBP price. Cash positions — which had been bolstered by equity raises in prior years — gave the company runway, not permanence.

The royalty inflection point remained contingent on a chain of events Ceres did not fully control: partners had to move from engineering prototype to certified product, then from certified product to commercial shipment volumes sufficient to generate material per-unit royalties. Until that chain completed, the company remained structurally dependent on milestone payments negotiated at inception rather than earned through market growth.

## One Dominant Relationship

The partnership structure that Caldwell built was geographically diverse on paper — Germany, South Korea, China, the Netherlands — but economically concentrated in ways that constituted a material risk in their own right.

Bosch, the German industrial conglomerate, was not merely a licensee. It held an equity stake in Ceres, participated in joint development programmes, and was positioned as the primary route to large-volume SOFC stack manufacturing in Europe. That depth of relationship — financial, technical, and strategic simultaneously — meant Bosch's trajectory was effectively Ceres's trajectory in Europe.

Should Bosch elect to slow investment in stationary SOFC products, restructure its energy division, or pivot capital toward competing electrochemical technologies, the consequences for Ceres's revenue and roadmap would be severe. The company had no obvious short-term substitute at comparable scale. Doosan provided Korean market exposure but operated in a different segment and at a different volume horizon. The diversification was real in a geographic sense; it was more limited in terms of near-term commercial weight.

The concentration risk was compounded by the licensing model itself. Because Ceres did not manufacture, it had no direct commercial channel of its own. Revenue required partners to sell. An unfavourable renegotiation, a partnership pause, or a strategic realignment by Bosch would propagate through Ceres's accounts with minimal buffer.

## The Pace Problem in SOFC Markets

The stationary fuel cell market grew through this period, but it grew unevenly and more slowly than optimistic projections from the early 2010s had suggested. Bloom Energy, the San José-based vertically integrated SOFC manufacturer, demonstrated that large-scale data centre and industrial deployments were commercially viable — but also showed how capital-intensive and operationally demanding that vertical model was. Ceres had deliberately chosen not to compete on Bloom's terrain, preferring the licensing route. The trade-off was that Ceres's commercial success depended entirely on its partners' willingness and ability to execute in a market that had not yet reached commodity scale.

Demand catalysts existed — rising interest in distributed generation, data centre power resilience, hydrogen-capable baseload — but the adoption curve for SOFC technology remained S-shaped in an uncomfortable way: visible inflection points always seemed to be one to two years ahead of where they actually materialised. Regulatory frameworks for distributed generation varied sharply by jurisdiction. Grid connectivity rules in Germany, permitting timelines in South Korea, and subsidy structures in China each created friction that slowed partner deployment cycles.

For a company whose royalty revenue depended on units shipped, market timing was not an abstraction. Each year's delay in commercial volume reduced the present value of the royalty stream and extended the period of net cash consumption.

## The Weichai Dimension

Weichai Power, the Shandong-headquartered engine manufacturer with deep ties to the Chinese state industrial apparatus, was both a major shareholder and a licensed partner. That dual role — strategic equity holder and commercial collaborator — created a structural entanglement that carried risks no engineering milestone could resolve.

The geopolitical environment surrounding UK-China technology relationships deteriorated materially over the years following Weichai's entry into Ceres's capital structure. Heightened scrutiny from HM Government of Chinese equity in strategically sensitive UK technology companies, combined with restrictions on technology transfer and export controls tightening on both sides of the Atlantic, raised questions about the durability of the arrangement in its current form.

Weichai's stake meant that Ceres's shareholder register included a significant Chinese state-adjacent investor in a company developing hydrogen and power technology increasingly considered dual-use. The company disclosed the relationship in statutory filings and maintained that partnership terms complied with applicable law. But the regulatory climate was not static, and the prospect of forced restructuring, transfer restrictions, or government intervention — however remote at any single point — was a scenario the market was required to price.

The Chinese market itself carried separate execution risk. Local distributed power deployments could not easily substitute for missing regulatory approvals or grid integration agreements. Weichai's ability to commercialise in China depended on domestic policy that Ceres could neither influence nor predict.

## Technology Execution at the Stack Level

SteelCell's steel-substrate architecture gave Ceres a manufacturing cost advantage over traditional ceramic SOFC designs — in principle. The practical challenge was proving that cost advantage at volume without sacrificing the degradation performance and thermal cycling durability that long-lived stationary applications required.

Fuel cell stacks do not degrade linearly. Small imperfections in cell manufacturing, interconnect sealing, or thermal management that are invisible at prototype scale can compound over thousands of operating hours. Ceres's engineering programme with Bosch and Doosan was partly about validating that the SteelCell could hit the field-life targets — typically expressed as percentage voltage degradation per thousand hours — that commercial buyers required. Until partners had multi-year field data from certified products in real installations, there remained residual uncertainty about long-term performance.

The SOEC electrolysis programme introduced additional execution complexity. Operating a solid oxide electrolyser at the pressures and temperatures required for efficient green hydrogen production pushed material science and system engineering in directions where Ceres had less accumulated field experience than it had with SOFC. The Shell partnership was scientifically promising; the commercial timeline was less certain.

## Governance, Dilution, and the AIM Premium

Ceres's capital structure reflected a business that had needed external funding at multiple stages. Equity raises — some at premium prices during the 2020–2021 hydrogen enthusiasm cycle, some at more modest levels — progressively diluted earlier shareholders. The company's listing on AIM rather than the Main Market meant it operated under a lighter disclosure regime, which suited the management team but gave institutional investors less standardised governance protection than they might require on a larger exchange.

The strategic equity positions held by Bosch and Weichai — both as partners and shareholders — raised questions about whose interests the board primarily served in moments of tension between commercial partnership terms and shareholder value. Non-executive independence on a small-cap AIM board with strategic anchor shareholders was structurally harder to maintain than governance codes aspired to.

Caldwell's tenure since 2013 created institutional continuity that the partnership relationships depended upon. It also meant the company carried succession risk concentrated in a single executive whose relationships with counterparts at Bosch, Doosan, Weichai, and Shell were not readily transferable. The technology was licensable. The trust built through a decade of partnership management was harder to replicate.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Twelve-Month Gauntlet

At the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, Ceres Power sits at a peculiar inflection point. The licensing model Phil Caldwell spent thirteen years constructing has four live commercial partnerships — Bosch, Doosan, Weichai, and Shell — but the architecture demands one thing above all else: partner volume. Engineering services fees and milestone payments cover the cost base; royalties, once partners reach commercial production thresholds, transform the economics entirely. The next twelve months will test whether the machinery built in Horsham can survive long enough to collect what it is owed.

---

## Earnings and Catalyst Calendar

The rhythm of disclosure on LSE AIM gives shareholders four meaningful windows between now and May 2027.

The Annual General Meeting, typically scheduled in late June, will be the first formal checkpoint after the frozen snapshot — expect a trading update accompanying the shareholder vote that frames H1 2026 progress across each partner programme. Historically Ceres uses AGM statements to signal engineering milestone completions and cash consumption rate without committing to quarterly guidance.

H1 2026 interim results land in September 2026. This is the most consequential single event in the window. The half-year report will disclose engineering services revenue recognised from Bosch and Weichai, any milestone payments triggered, and — critically — the closing cash position against a guided full-year burn rate. If Bosch's SteelCell manufacturing programme at its German facility hits internal qualification targets, Ceres could recognise a milestone payment in H1, lifting reported revenue materially above the prior comparable period.

A capital markets event or investor day, if scheduled, would most likely fall in autumn 2026. Ceres has periodically used such forums to update on partner volume trajectories and provide SteelCell stack performance data that validates the licensing thesis. Any such event would likely include technology demonstrations and Bosch deployment data.

Full-year 2026 results follow in March or April 2027. This report closes the financial loop on the twelve-month window and is the first opportunity to confirm whether FY 2026 met the revenue and cash targets management set at the beginning of the year.

---

## Partner Milestones: The Specific Gates

**Bosch (Germany — SOFC stationary power):** The dominant revenue and thesis catalyst. Bosch holds a strategic equity stake in Ceres and is the primary near-term royalty source. The critical unknown at the frozen snapshot is the cadence of Bosch's manufacturing qualification — the transition from validated engineering samples to commercial series production at its German facility. Each SteelCell stack qualification tier triggers milestone revenue under the licence agreement. Specifically, watch for: first commercial delivery confirmation (Q3 or Q4 2026 is the analyst consensus expectation); commencement of recurring royalty payments, which require Bosch to invoice customer volumes; and any Bosch earnings commentary on fuel cell programme capex, which signals internal confidence. Bosch's own capital allocation decisions — particularly in the context of its 2024–2026 cost restructuring — remain the single largest exogenous risk to Ceres's timeline.

**Weichai Power (China — distributed power):** China's regulatory environment for distributed SOFC power and hydrogen adds complexity absent in the Bosch pathway. Weichai's ability to deploy SteelCell-based systems into the Chinese market depends partly on domestic certification approvals. Watch for any National Energy Administration pilot approvals for stationary SOFC in H2 2026, as well as Weichai's own disclosure of deployment units and cumulative installed capacity. The milestone structure in the Weichai agreement means Ceres receives payments tied to design completion and initial production rather than volume, making near-term recognition more predictable — but the long-term royalty case depends on Chinese market penetration Ceres cannot control.

**Shell (SOEC — green hydrogen):** The Shell partnership sits on a longer development timeline than the SOFC programmes. Solid oxide electrolyser cell technology for green hydrogen is earlier-stage commercially. The twelve-month catalyst here is not revenue but programme validation: Shell presenting SOEC stack performance data internally or at hydrogen industry conferences would raise the probability of progression to demonstration-scale deployment. Any public Shell commentary on scaling its electrolyser supply chain — including references to solid oxide versus alkaline or PEM technology selection — would be a meaningful signal for Ceres's longer-term book.

**Doosan (Korea — stationary power):** Doosan's partnership has historically generated engineering services revenue on a lower trajectory than Bosch. Korean stationary fuel cell regulation has been broadly supportive, but Doosan's own balance sheet pressures post-2020 restructuring created uncertainty. Watch for any Korea Smart Power programme tender awards that specify SOFC technology and Doosan bid participation.

---

## Financial Estimates and Implied Growth

Ceres does not issue detailed quarterly guidance, and the AIM disclosure framework does not compel it. The consensus analyst range — drawn from coverage at Peel Hunt, Berenberg, and Canaccord Genuity, which collectively provide most sellside research on the stock — implies the following framework for the twelve-month window:

| Period | Revenue (consensus midpoint) | YoY Growth | Operating loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 2026 | £9–12m | +5–15% | (£12–15m) |
| H2 2026 | £11–14m | +10–25% | (£10–13m) |
| FY 2026 | £20–26m | +8–20% | (£22–28m) |
| FY 2027E | £28–38m | +30–50% | (£15–22m) |

Revenue growth in FY 2026 is primarily a function of Bosch milestone timing; the FY 2027 step-up is where analyst models diverge most significantly, conditional on Bosch royalties commencing. Cash on the balance sheet at year-end 2025 — disclosed in the March 2026 annual results — sets the available runway. Management has historically guided to eighteen to twenty-four months of runway from any given reporting date.

---

## Beat Versus Miss: The Specific Metrics

A **beat** in September's H1 report requires three things landing together: (1) milestone revenue from Bosch above the implied H1 phasing in consensus models, likely reflecting engineering qualification completion ahead of schedule; (2) group cash at 30 June 2026 ahead of the implied burn trajectory, suggesting partner payments arrived in Q2 rather than Q3; and (3) Caldwell providing forward language on Bosch commercial volume timing that is more specific than prior disclosures — phrases like "targeted first commercial deliveries by mid-2027" would be more bullish than current guidance signals.

A **miss** is characterised by: milestone payment slippage into H2 or FY 2027; a cash position that implies an equity raise within six to nine months; or Bosch commentary — via its own earnings channel — that pauses or phases back the fuel cell programme in response to market demand weakness or internal capital prioritisation.

---

## The Bull and Bear Asymmetry

The bull case is structural. If Bosch reaches series production in H2 2026 or early 2027 and triggers royalty payments, the per-unit economics of the SteelCell licensing model produce revenue with near-zero incremental cost for Ceres. Consensus models that assume FY 2027 royalty commencement imply a revenue inflection that would take the company toward cash-flow breakeven by FY 2028 without requiring further dilutive equity. Weichai adds a second, slower royalty track into a market an order of magnitude larger. Shell adds optionality on the electrolyser market at no cost to the existing income statement.

> "We have built the technology platform, the partnerships and the team to become the leading fuel cell and electrolysis technology licensor globally. Our focus is now on working closely with our partners to drive to commercial volumes."

That framing from Caldwell — representing the consistent management posture across multiple earnings calls — encapsulates the bull thesis: patience and leverage.

The bear case is equally structural. The licensing model transfers manufacturing risk to partners but also transfers volume control. Ceres cannot compel Bosch to produce faster, cannot accelerate Weichai's Chinese regulatory approvals, and cannot substitute a new partner if the existing anchor relationship slows. Each month of delay in Bosch series production burns cash that required either equity issuance or milestone negotiation to replace. At the frozen snapshot, the company's share price already prices in meaningful scepticism about the royalty commencement timeline — but a second Bosch programme delay, or an equity raise at a discount, would reset that floor lower.

The asymmetry, at 23 May 2026, favours the bull case on a probability-weighted basis only if Bosch's manufacturing programme holds its current internal schedule. The margin for error is thin, and the next four reporting events are the instrument by which that margin will be measured.

chapters.title: Royalty inflection, SOEC scaling, additional partner deals, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
The year 2025 will be remembered inside Ceres Power's Horsham headquarters not for its revenue line — which fell to £32.6 million from £51.9 million a year earlier, a 37 per cent decline — but for two words buried near the bottom of the income statement: royalty income. The amount was £110,000. In the context of a company that had spent two decades and hundreds of millions of pounds developing a solid oxide platform licensed to manufacturing partners across three continents, it was barely a rounding error. Phil Caldwell, chief executive since 2013, understood what it signalled. "Doosan's start of mass manufacture of Ceres-based products," he told investors in [March 2026 final results](https://www.ceres.tech/media/jpmpucda/ceres-power-holdings-plc-final-results-statement-2026-march-26.pdf), marked "a key inflection point as the company transitions from an R&D-led organisation to a commercially focused business." First royalties are almost never large. They are almost always transformative in what they prove.

## The Bosch Rupture and the Cost of Concentration

Before the inflection point could be framed as a clean narrative, Ceres had to absorb the most significant single setback in its commercial history. On a February morning in 2025, Robert Bosch GmbH informed Caldwell that it was ending its multi-year strategic partnership in solid oxide fuel cell industrialisation — and that it would sell its 17.44 per cent equity stake. The disclosure sent Ceres shares down 42 per cent in a single session to 75.75p, a collapse that illustrated just how much the market had priced the German engineering giant as a cornerstone validation.

Bosch's explanation was candid to the point of being uncomfortable. The SOFC market, it said, had "not developed as expected," with customer demand shifting toward higher-output systems with carbon capture, making "the conditions for economical operation significantly tougher." The priority was shifting to hydrogen electrolysis, not generation. [Ceres maintained its composure in public.](https://www.proactiveinvestors.co.uk/companies/news/1066591/ceres-power-plunges-as-bosch-ends-partnership-amid-strategic-shift-1066591.html) "Whilst Ceres is disappointed that Bosch will discontinue its operations relating to the industrialisation and preparation for production of decentralised power-supply systems using Ceres' solid oxide technology," Caldwell said in the RNS, "we recognise that this decision is part of a broader revised strategic direction from Bosch and does not reflect its confidence around Ceres or our technology."

The language was careful and the distinction was real: Bosch was exiting stationary natural-gas SOFC, not repudiating solid oxide as a technology class. But the structural problem was exposed nonetheless. Ceres had been running a licensing model whose commercial momentum — and market capitalisation — was disproportionately tethered to a single Tier 1 backer. The Bosch withdrawal did not alter Ceres' 2025 consensus expectations, analysts noted, because the partnership had already been winding down at the engineering services level. But it reshuffled the narrative. The 2026-2030 story would have to be built around different anchors.

## Doosan: The First Royalty and the Korean Anchor

The anchor that mattered most by the second half of 2025 was Doosan Fuel Cell. In July 2025, Doosan formally commenced mass production of solid oxide fuel cell power systems at a new facility in South Korea with 50 MW of annual manufacturing capacity — the first partner site built specifically to industrial scale using [Ceres SteelCell technology](https://www.ceres.tech/newsroom/news-and-insights/doosan-fuel-cell-begins-mass-production-of-fuel-cell-power-systems-using-ceres-technology/). The milestone triggered the first royalty payments to Ceres: £110,000 recognised in the 2025 full-year accounts, a sum whose symbolic weight vastly exceeded its nominal value.

The timing aligned with a structural shift in the demand environment that neither Ceres nor Doosan had fully anticipated when they deepened their collaboration. The surge in artificial-intelligence infrastructure investment had created an acute problem for data centre operators: power availability. Doosan Fuel Cell — whose stock gained nearly 25 per cent on the mass-production announcement — had positioned its SOFC systems as a dispatchable, low-emissions on-site generation solution directly competing for data centre backup and primary-power contracts. Caldwell described the convergence bluntly in his year-end statement, noting "unprecedented change in the market with acute demand for power to service AI data centres" arriving precisely as Doosan's production lines came online.

The royalty arithmetic underpinning the 2026-2030 thesis flows directly from this ramp. Analyst estimates at Berenberg suggest that a single licensing partner scaling to 1 GW of annual production under Ceres' Endura technology framework could generate between £50 million and £100 million in annual royalty revenue — a figure that would, at prevailing sector multiples, represent approximately $1 billion in shareholder value creation in isolation. Doosan's 50 MW facility is one fiftieth of that threshold. But it is operating, generating royalties, and targeting the fastest-growing segment of global electricity demand.

## Weichai and the China Manufacturing Licence

On 5 November 2025, Ceres announced the signing of a manufacturing licence agreement with Weichai Power, the Shandong-based diesel engine and powertrain conglomerate that had been a Ceres partner since 2019. The new agreement granted Weichai rights to [produce Ceres SOFC cells and stacks at a dedicated facility in China](https://www.ceres.tech/media/2dtcn4ns/weichai-signs-manufacturing-licence-for-sofc-power-rns.pdf), mirroring the production-scale structure already in place with Doosan in Korea. Ceres retains responsibility for supplying certain proprietary cell components — a design that preserves the technology transfer boundary and keeps royalty economics visible — while receiving upfront licence fees, milestone payments, and ongoing per-unit royalties as production scales.

Licence revenues from the Weichai agreement were guided to begin being recognised in the first half of 2026. The deal addressed a strategic question that the Bosch exit had made more pressing: could Ceres maintain geographic breadth without a German anchor? The answer, partly, was China. Weichai's access to Chinese manufacturing cost structures and distribution in distributed power markets represents a different commercial pathway from the Korean data-centre play, but the royalty mechanics are structurally identical.

## Delta Electronics and the SOEC Dimension

The £43 million Delta Electronics licence signed in January 2024 — Ceres' first explicit hydrogen-electrolysis commercial agreement — moved from deal into product development phase through 2025. Under the agreement, the Taiwanese power electronics manufacturer committed to integrating Ceres' solid oxide electrolyser cell technology with its own thermal management systems at its Tainan manufacturing complex, with [production targeted for commencement by end-2026](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20240118VL207/delta-electronics-ceres-power-hydrogen-energy-fuel-cell.html). Approximately half the £43 million — roughly £21.5 million — was recognised as revenue in 2024; the remainder flows through engineering services and milestone payments as the Tainan line is commissioned.

Delta's entry into the Ceres partner ecosystem was significant beyond its deal value. It was the first licence explicitly spanning both SOFC and SOEC applications, and it came from a manufacturer with established relationships in the data centre power infrastructure market. Delta builds power management systems for some of the largest hyperscale facilities in Asia. The prospect of that distribution network accessing Ceres-derived electrolyser systems — producing green hydrogen for on-site industrial use — extends the potential royalty base beyond stationary power into process chemistry, metals, and heavy transport decarbonisation.

## Shell's Bangalore Milestone

The clearest proof-of-concept for the SOEC pathway came in May 2025, when Shell and Ceres announced that hydrogen was being produced at [Shell's Technology Centre in Bangalore](https://www.ceres.tech/newsroom/news-and-insights/shell-ceres-mw-scale-electrolyser-project-produces-first-hydrogen/) — the site of their joint MW-scale SOEC demonstrator, the first system of its kind operating in India. At full capacity, the electrolyser is capable of producing 600 kilograms of hydrogen per day, with a module-level efficiency of 37 kWh/kg — within range of the EU's stated 2030 target of sub-36 kWh/kg and approximately 35 per cent more hydrogen output per unit of electricity than competing polymer-electrolyte-membrane systems when co-located with industrial heat sources.

The Bangalore demonstrator does not generate royalties. Its function is validation: it establishes that Ceres' metal-supported cell design operates at lower temperatures than conventional solid oxide systems, demonstrating the durability and cost characteristics that would underpin a commercial electrolyser licensing agreement should Shell elect to proceed to production scale. The programme, running since 2022, has systematically de-risked the SOEC technology stack in an operating industrial environment. The question for 2026 and beyond is whether Shell translates demonstrator success into a manufacturing commitment comparable to Doosan's in Korea.

## Centrica, Delta, and the Data Centre Service Model

In March 2026 — just within the chapter's frozen window — Ceres disclosed a strategic partnership with [Centrica](https://www.centrica.com/media-centre/news/2026/centrica-and-ceres-sign-strategic-partnership-to-bring-multi-gw-on-site-fuel-cell-power-to-the-uk-and-europe/), the British energy and services group, targeting multi-gigawatt deployment of on-site fuel cell power across the UK and European market. A subsequent announcement in April 2026 confirmed that Delta Electronics had joined as the manufacturing partner in a three-way structure: Ceres provides technology, Delta manufactures stacks and systems, and Centrica originates projects, handles installation, commissioning, remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, and end-of-life recycling. The model is explicitly service-led — Centrica's energy supply and trading platform absorbs the customer-facing complexity, allowing Ceres and Delta to focus on technology performance.

The data centre application is central to the Centrica-Delta-Ceres thesis. High-density computing facilities require dispatchable power with low grid-dependency, high reliability, and a credible emissions profile. Solid oxide fuel cells — operating on natural gas in the near term, hydrogen-ready as supply chains mature — offer a differentiated proposition against both diesel backup generation and battery storage at the multi-megawatt scale.

## Royalty Geometry and the 2026-2030 Horizon

Ceres enters its 2026-2030 phase with contracted revenue of approximately £45 million before any incremental new business, a cash position of £83.3 million, and a cash outflow that fell to £19.2 million in 2025 from £37.5 million in 2024. The company's gross margin held at 70 per cent on the reduced revenue base, reflecting the structural advantage of a licensing model: when engineering services revenue shrinks, margin does not collapse because the cost base is not vertically integrated against production volumes.

| Partner | Application | Status at May 2026 | Royalty stage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Doosan (Korea) | Stationary power / data centre | 50 MW in mass production | Royalties commenced (£110k, 2025) |
| Weichai (China) | Distributed power | Manufacturing licence signed Nov 2025 | Licence fees H1 2026 → royalties on production |
| Delta Electronics (Taiwan) | SOFC + SOEC / data centre | Product development, production target end-2026 | Engineering milestones → royalties post-2026 |
| Shell (global) | Green hydrogen / SOEC | MW demonstrator producing hydrogen in Bangalore | Pre-commercial; licensing terms unconfirmed |
| Centrica / Delta (UK-Europe) | Data centre / heavy industry | Partnership signed March-April 2026 | Deployment-dependent royalties, medium term |

The transition from fees to royalties will not be smooth. Each partner's ramp follows its own capex cycle, regulatory environment, and end-market demand curve. Doosan's 50 MW facility in Korea is a beginning, not a destination. Weichai's manufacturing line in China is not yet producing cells. Delta's Tainan plant is being commissioned. The Centrica deployment pipeline exists on paper.

But the structure of the 2026-2030 horizon is clearer than at any prior point in Ceres' 25-year history. The company has survived the loss of its most prominent European partner, recognised its first royalties, signed a Chinese manufacturing licence, validated MW-scale electrolysis in a live industrial environment, and entered the data centre market through a three-way commercial model that it could not have assembled without a decade of engineering credibility. Caldwell's framing of 2025 as an inflection year was not investor relations language. It was a description of mechanism: the model is no longer hypothetical. The royalties — all £110,000 of them — have begun.

---
